title: Binary Search Visualization — Watch lo, hi and mid Move
metaDescription: Run binary search on real C++ and watch lo, hi and mid move each iteration. Includes the off-by-one bugs that cause infinite loops, and how to spot them.
intro: Halving a search space sounds trivial until you write it and the loop never ends. The algorithm is four lines; the hard part is the boundary arithmetic, which is why almost everyone gets it wrong at least once. Watching lo, hi and mid change on every pass makes the failure modes obvious in a way that reading the code never does.
codeNote: Classic inclusive-bounds binary search: it returns the index of 23 (which is 5) and -1 for 7, which is absent.

howItWorks.heading: The invariant does the work
howItWorks.body: At every moment, if the target exists it lies inside a[lo..hi]. Every line in the loop is written to preserve that one sentence. If you ever break it, the search silently returns -1 for values that are actually present.

howItWorks.heading: Probe the middle, not the front
howItWorks.body: mid splits the live range in half. Comparing a[mid] to the target tells you which half can still contain it, so one comparison eliminates the other half entirely — that is where the log n comes from.

howItWorks.heading: Move past mid, never onto it
howItWorks.body: When a[mid] < target, the answer cannot be at mid, so lo becomes mid + 1. Setting lo = mid instead leaves mid inside the range forever and the loop stops shrinking.

howItWorks.heading: lo <= hi is the termination condition
howItWorks.body: The range is inclusive on both ends, so lo == hi still holds exactly one candidate and must be checked. The loop ends when lo passes hi, meaning the live range is empty and the target is absent.

howItWorks.heading: Why mid is computed that way
howItWorks.body: lo + (hi - lo) / 2 is arithmetically the same as (lo + hi) / 2 but never overflows, because hi - lo fits in an int even when lo + hi would not. On a 10-element array it makes no difference; on indices near 2 billion it does.

complexity.note: Each iteration discards half the remaining range, so the loop runs at most log2(n) times; it degrades to useless (not slow — wrong) the instant the input is not sorted by the same comparison the branches use.

gotchas.title: The lo = mid infinite loop
gotchas.body: Writing lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 hangs the program whenever hi == lo + 1: mid rounds down to lo, the condition picks the upper half, and lo is reassigned to the value it already had. Nothing changes and the loop spins forever. Run it in DryRun and you see lo, hi and mid freeze at the same three numbers on frame after frame — that repeated state is the bug, and it is much faster to spot than to reason about.

gotchas.title: int hi = a.size() - 1 on an empty vector
gotchas.body: size() returns an unsigned type, so 0 - 1 wraps to a huge value before the conversion to int. On an empty vector you get an enormous or negative hi and then an out-of-bounds read at a[mid]. Cast first: int hi = (int)a.size() - 1.

gotchas.title: Using < instead of <= in the loop condition
gotchas.body: With inclusive bounds, while (lo < hi) skips the final one-element range. The search returns -1 for any target that happens to land at the last surviving index — it works on most test cases and fails on a few, which is the worst kind of bug.

gotchas.title: Searching data that is not actually sorted
gotchas.body: Binary search does not detect unsorted input; it just returns -1 or the wrong index. This bites hardest when you sort by one key (say, by name) and then search by another (by id). Print or inspect the array right before the call rather than trusting the sort you wrote three functions earlier.

faq.q: Why does binary search need a sorted array?
faq.a: Because the algorithm throws away half the array based on a single comparison, and that decision is only valid if order guarantees where the target can be. If a[mid] < target in a sorted array, every element left of mid is also smaller, so none of them can match. In unsorted data that inference is false and you discard elements that may contain the answer.

faq.q: Why is binary search O(log n)?
faq.a: Each iteration halves the number of candidates: n, then n/2, then n/4, and so on. The number of halvings needed to reach a single element is log2(n), so a million-element array takes about 20 comparisons instead of a million.

faq.q: What causes an infinite loop in binary search?
faq.a: An iteration that fails to shrink the range. The usual culprit is lo = mid or hi = mid instead of mid + 1 or mid - 1, which lets mid stay inside the live range when lo and hi are adjacent. Every path through the loop must strictly reduce hi - lo.

faq.q: Should I use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 or (lo + hi) / 2?
faq.a: Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2. The two are mathematically identical, but (lo + hi) can overflow a signed int when both indices are large, producing a negative mid and an out-of-bounds access. This is the bug that sat in the JDK binary search for nearly a decade.

faq.q: Can binary search work on a linked list?
faq.a: Not usefully. Binary search depends on O(1) random access to reach mid; in a linked list, walking to the middle costs O(n), so each of the log n steps becomes linear and you end up slower than a plain scan.

title: Linear Search Visualization — The Baseline Everything Is Measured Against
metaDescription: See linear search scan an array element by element in real C++, why it is sometimes the right answer, and the early-return bugs hiding inside it.
intro: Checking every element until you find what you want is the algorithm you would invent on your own, which is exactly why it is worth understanding precisely. It needs no preprocessing, no sorted input, and no assumptions — and for small or unsorted data it frequently beats the clever alternatives once you count the cost of sorting.
codeNote: Returns the index of the first match — note that 7 appears twice and the search stops at index 1, never seeing index 3.

howItWorks.heading: One pass, one comparison per element
howItWorks.body: The index i walks from 0 upward and each element is tested exactly once. There is no state to maintain beyond i, which is why the function is trivially correct and almost impossible to get subtly wrong.

howItWorks.heading: Returning early is the whole optimisation
howItWorks.body: return i inside the loop means the function stops the moment it succeeds. On average a present target is found halfway through, so the expected work is n/2 comparisons even though the worst case is n.

howItWorks.heading: Absence costs full price
howItWorks.body: A missing target forces the loop to run to completion. If most of your lookups are misses, linear search performs at its worst case every single time — that asymmetry is what usually justifies switching to a hash set or a sorted array.

howItWorks.heading: First match, not best match
howItWorks.body: The function returns the earliest index that matches. If you need the last occurrence, the count, or all positions, the loop body has to change; swapping in a different search algorithm will not fix it.

howItWorks.heading: Why it survives
howItWorks.body: It works on unsorted data, on linked structures, on streams you can only read once, and on comparisons that are not orderings (matching by predicate rather than by <). None of the faster searches do all of that.

complexity.time: O(n) worst and average, O(1) best
complexity.note: Every element may need one comparison, so time scales linearly; it stays O(n) no matter how the data is arranged, which makes it predictable but means it never improves with repeated queries the way a sorted array or hash table does.

gotchas.title: Comparing a signed i against an unsigned size()
gotchas.body: for (int i = 0; i < a.size(); i++) makes the compiler promote i to unsigned. It works, but it emits a warning and turns any negative index arithmetic you add later into a wraparound to billions. Cast the size or use size_t deliberately — pick one and be consistent.

gotchas.title: Returning 0 instead of -1 for not found
gotchas.body: Zero is a perfectly valid index, so a caller writing if (linearSearch(...)) treats a hit at index 0 as a miss. Use -1, or return a boolean plus an out-parameter. This bug survives every test case where the target is not first.

gotchas.title: Forgetting that the return exits the whole function
gotchas.body: People often add a counter after the loop to tally matches and cannot work out why it is always 0 or 1. The early return leaves the function on the first hit. If you want to count, drop the return and accumulate — stepping through shows execution leaving the function on iteration 1.

gotchas.title: Reaching for binary search too early
gotchas.body: If you sort an unsorted array just to run one binary search, you have paid O(n log n) to save O(n). Sorting only pays off when you will search the same array many times. Measure the number of queries before you optimise the search.

faq.q: When is linear search better than binary search?
faq.a: When the data is unsorted and you will only search it once or twice, because sorting first costs more than the scan you avoided. It is also better for very small arrays — under roughly 20 to 50 elements the simple loop wins on real hardware thanks to cache locality and branch prediction, regardless of the asymptotics.

faq.q: What is the time complexity of linear search?
faq.a: O(n) in the worst and average case, O(1) in the best case when the target is the first element. A failed search always costs the full n comparisons because the loop cannot conclude the item is absent until it has checked everything.

faq.q: Does linear search work on unsorted data?
faq.a: Yes, and that is its main advantage. It makes no assumption about order because it tests every element individually rather than inferring anything from position. That also means it works with equality-only comparisons where no ordering exists.

faq.q: How do I find all occurrences instead of the first?
faq.a: Remove the early return and push each matching index into a result vector, returning it after the loop. The scan then always costs a full O(n) pass since it cannot stop early, and the caller gets every position rather than just the earliest.

title: Bubble Sort Step by Step — Watch Every Swap Happen
metaDescription: Watch bubble sort compare and swap adjacent pairs in real C++, see why the largest element lands last on every pass, and fix the classic bounds bugs.
intro: Repeatedly swapping neighbours that are out of order is the least efficient way to sort anything, and also the clearest window into what sorting actually is. Every pass drags the biggest remaining value to the end, which is why it is worth watching once: the mechanism is visible in a way that quicksort's partitioning never is.
code: for (int i = 0; i < n - 1 - pass; i++) {
codeNote: The optimised version: the inner loop shrinks each pass, and the swapped flag exits early once a full pass makes no changes.

howItWorks.heading: Only adjacent pairs are ever compared
howItWorks.body: The inner loop looks at a[i] and a[i+1] and nothing else. A value can therefore move at most one position per comparison, which is precisely why the algorithm is slow — an element at the front that belongs at the back needs n-1 separate swaps to get there.

howItWorks.heading: Each pass parks one element permanently
howItWorks.body: Follow the largest value: once the scan reaches it, every subsequent comparison swaps it forward, so it rides to the end of the pass in one continuous sweep. After pass k, the last k positions hold the k largest values in final order.

howItWorks.heading: That is why the inner loop shrinks
howItWorks.body: n - 1 - pass stops the scan before the already-sorted tail. Without it the algorithm still works but wastes a growing number of guaranteed-false comparisons on every pass.

howItWorks.heading: The swapped flag detects sortedness
howItWorks.body: If an entire pass makes zero swaps, no adjacent pair is out of order, and an array with no out-of-order adjacent pairs is sorted. That turns the best case for nearly-sorted input from O(n squared) into a single O(n) verification pass.

howItWorks.heading: Stability comes from the strict comparison
howItWorks.body: The swap only fires on a[i] > a[i+1], never on equality, so equal elements never cross each other. Change it to >= and you break stability while doing strictly more work.

complexity.time: O(n squared) average and worst, O(n) best with the early exit
complexity.note: There are roughly n squared over 2 comparisons because each of n passes scans most of the array; the best case only reaches O(n) if you keep the swapped flag, and the worst case (a reversed array) forces every single swap.

gotchas.title: Off-by-one at a[i + 1]
gotchas.body: Writing for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) with a[i + 1] inside reads one element past the end on the last iteration. In C++ that is undefined behaviour and often appears to work — the vector has spare capacity and you read garbage that happens to be large. The bound must be n - 1 - pass.

gotchas.title: Losing a value in a hand-written swap
gotchas.body: a[i] = a[i+1]; a[i+1] = a[i]; overwrites a[i] before it is saved, so both slots end up holding the same value and the original is gone. Watching the array in a step-through makes it unmistakable: a duplicate appears and an element vanishes. Use a temporary, or std::swap.

gotchas.title: Declaring swapped outside the outer loop
gotchas.body: If bool swapped = false lives above the pass loop, it stays true forever after the first swap and the early exit never fires. Worse, some people set it true once and check it inverted, which exits after pass one and leaves the array half-sorted. It must be reset at the top of every pass.

gotchas.title: int n = a.size() then looping to n - 1 on an empty vector
gotchas.body: For an empty or single-element vector, n - 1 is 0 or -1 and the loops correctly do nothing — but only because n is a signed int. If you write a.size() - 1 directly in the condition, the unsigned wraparound produces a gigantic bound and the function walks off the end.

faq.q: Why is bubble sort so slow?
faq.a: Because elements move only one position per swap. An element that needs to travel from the front to the back requires n-1 individual swaps, and with n elements potentially needing that, the total work is proportional to n squared. Algorithms like merge sort move elements large distances in a single step, which is the entire difference.

faq.q: Is bubble sort ever actually used?
faq.a: Almost never in production, but it has one genuine niche: detecting whether a nearly-sorted array is already in order. With the swapped-flag optimisation it confirms sortedness in a single O(n) pass and touches no memory beyond the array itself. Real libraries use insertion sort for that job instead, since it handles small disorder just as cheaply and degrades far better.

faq.q: What is the difference between bubble sort and selection sort?
faq.a: Bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs repeatedly, so it performs many swaps but can stop early when the array is sorted. Selection sort scans for the minimum and performs exactly one swap per pass, so it does far fewer writes but always runs the full n squared comparisons regardless of the input.

faq.q: Is bubble sort stable?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the comparison is strictly greater-than. Equal elements are never swapped past each other, so their original relative order survives. Changing the condition to >= makes it unstable and adds pointless swaps.

title: Selection Sort Visualization — Fewest Swaps, Most Comparisons
metaDescription: Watch selection sort find the minimum and place it, in real running C++. See why it always costs n squared comparisons and why it is not stable.
intro: Find the smallest thing, put it at the front, repeat on what remains. Selection sort is the sorting method humans instinctively use on a hand of cards, and it has one genuinely useful property: it performs at most n swaps total, which matters when writing is expensive and reading is cheap.
code: for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
codeNote: Tracks the index of the minimum rather than its value, then performs at most one swap per outer iteration.

howItWorks.heading: The array splits into sorted and unsorted
howItWorks.body: Everything before index i is finished and will never be touched again. Everything from i onward is the unsorted remainder. The outer loop grows the sorted prefix by exactly one element per iteration.

howItWorks.heading: The inner loop only records a position
howItWorks.body: It does not move anything. It scans the unsorted remainder and remembers where the smallest value lives. Tracking the index rather than the value matters — you need to know where to swap from, not just what the minimum is.

howItWorks.heading: One swap places the element for good
howItWorks.body: After the scan, a single exchange puts the minimum at index i and pushes whatever was there into the vacated slot. That element is now in its final position; no later pass can move it.

howItWorks.heading: The last element is free
howItWorks.body: The outer loop runs to n - 1, not n. Once the first n-1 positions hold the n-1 smallest values in order, the single remaining element must be the largest and is already where it belongs.

howItWorks.heading: The comparison count never changes
howItWorks.body: The inner loop always scans the entire remainder regardless of what it finds, so a sorted array and a reversed array cost exactly the same number of comparisons. There is no early exit to add — the algorithm has no way to know it is done.

complexity.note: The nested scans always perform n(n-1)/2 comparisons because the inner loop cannot stop early; what it buys you is at most n-1 swaps, versus up to n squared for bubble sort, which matters when a write costs far more than a read.

gotchas.title: Storing the minimum value instead of its index
gotchas.body: int minVal = a[i]; then updating minVal in the loop leaves you with the right number and no idea where it came from. The swap needs a position. Track minIdx and read a[minIdx] when you need the value.

gotchas.title: Forgetting to reset minIdx each pass
gotchas.body: If minIdx = i sits above the outer loop, the second pass starts comparing against a stale position — usually an element already locked into the sorted prefix — so the scan finds nothing smaller and the array stops sorting after the first element. Step through pass two and watch minIdx never move.

gotchas.title: Starting the inner loop at j = i instead of j = i + 1
gotchas.body: It still produces a correct result, since comparing a[i] against itself changes nothing, but it wastes one comparison per pass. Harmless here, genuinely wrong if you later adapt the same loop shape to find a strict second-smallest.

gotchas.title: Assuming selection sort is stable
gotchas.body: It is not. Sorting the pairs (5a, 5b, 2) puts 2 at the front by swapping it with 5a, which throws 5a behind 5b and reverses their original order. If stability matters, use insertion sort or merge sort — no amount of tweaking the comparison fixes this, because the long-distance swap is the mechanism itself.

faq.q: Why does selection sort always take O(n squared) time?
faq.a: Because the inner loop has to examine every remaining element to be sure it has found the minimum, and there is no way to conclude early. An already-sorted array still requires all n(n-1)/2 comparisons. Unlike bubble sort or insertion sort, it has no best case.

faq.q: Is selection sort faster than bubble sort?
faq.a: In practice usually yes, though both are O(n squared). Selection sort performs at most n-1 swaps while bubble sort can perform O(n squared) of them, and writes are typically more expensive than comparisons. Bubble sort only wins on data that is already nearly sorted, where its early-exit check finishes in one pass.

faq.q: Is selection sort stable?
faq.a: No. The swap moves the minimum across arbitrary distance, jumping it over elements equal to the one it displaces, which reverses their relative order. A stable variant exists that shifts elements instead of swapping, but then you have lost the low-swap-count advantage and effectively written insertion sort.

faq.q: When would I choose selection sort?
faq.a: When writes are far more expensive than reads — flash memory with limited write cycles, or sorting records that are costly to move. It guarantees at most n-1 writes to the array, a bound no comparison sort with better time complexity offers.

title: Insertion Sort Visualization — Why Real Libraries Still Use It
metaDescription: See insertion sort shift elements to make room, in real running C++. Learn why it beats quicksort on small arrays and how the shifting loop goes wrong.
intro: Take the next element, slide it backwards past everything larger, drop it in place. This is how you sort a hand of cards, and unlike its O(n squared) siblings it earns its keep in production: std::sort switches to insertion sort once a partition gets small, because on short or nearly-sorted runs it genuinely is the fastest thing available.
codeNote: Shifts larger elements right one at a time rather than swapping, so each element is written once per position it passes.

howItWorks.heading: The prefix is always sorted
howItWorks.body: Before iteration i, a[0..i-1] is sorted among itself — though not necessarily in final position, since a later element may still need to slide into the middle of it. The loop starts at 1 because a single element is trivially sorted.

howItWorks.heading: key is saved before the shifting starts
howItWorks.body: a[i] is copied into key first, which frees that slot. The while loop then overwrites it with the shifted neighbour. Without the copy, the first shift would destroy the value you are trying to place.

howItWorks.heading: Shifting, not swapping
howItWorks.body: Each larger element moves one slot right, opening a gap that travels leftwards. This is roughly half the memory traffic of a swap-based version, which does three writes per step instead of one — the reason this beats bubble sort on identical comparison counts.

howItWorks.heading: The while loop stops at the right place twice over
howItWorks.body: It exits either because j hit -1 (key is the new smallest) or because a[j] <= key (the correct spot). Both cases leave the gap at j + 1, which is why a single a[j + 1] = key handles them both.

howItWorks.heading: Nearly-sorted input barely moves
howItWorks.body: If each element is already close to its final position, the while loop runs a couple of iterations and stops. Total work becomes O(n + d) where d is the number of inversions, so an almost-sorted array is handled in near-linear time.

complexity.time: O(n squared) worst, O(n) best, O(n + inversions) in general
complexity.note: The inner loop runs once per inversion involving the current element, so a reversed array costs the full n squared while a sorted one costs a single comparison per element; that adaptivity is exactly why library sorts fall back to it below ~16 elements.

gotchas.title: Writing a[j] = key instead of a[j + 1] = key
gotchas.body: When the while loop exits, j points one slot to the left of the gap — either at the element that is <= key, or at -1. Writing to a[j] either clobbers a correctly placed value or, when j is -1, corrupts memory before the array. The gap is always at j + 1.

gotchas.title: Checking a[j] > key before checking j >= 0
gotchas.body: Reversing the operands to while (a[j] > key && j >= 0) reads a[-1] when key is the smallest element seen so far. C++ short-circuits left to right, so the bounds test must come first. This crashes only on inputs with a new minimum, which is why it survives casual testing.

gotchas.title: Starting the outer loop at i = 0
gotchas.body: Then j starts at -1, the while loop is skipped, and a[0] = key rewrites the element with itself. Harmless, but it signals a misunderstanding: the first element is the initial sorted prefix, not something to insert.

gotchas.title: Using >= in the shift condition
gotchas.body: while (j >= 0 && a[j] >= key) keeps shifting past elements equal to key, placing the new element before its equals and destroying stability. It also does strictly more work. Insertion sort is stable precisely because it stops at the first element that is not greater.

faq.q: Why is insertion sort used inside real sorting libraries?
faq.a: Because for small arrays it is genuinely fastest. It has almost no per-element overhead, excellent cache behaviour since it touches adjacent memory, and it exploits partial order. Implementations of std::sort run introsort down to a threshold of roughly 16 elements and then finish the whole array with one insertion sort pass.

faq.q: What is the difference between insertion sort and bubble sort?
faq.a: Insertion sort takes one element and moves it directly to its correct place in the sorted prefix, shifting others aside. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent pairs across the whole array. They have the same worst-case complexity, but insertion sort does about a third of the writes and adapts far better to nearly-sorted input.

faq.q: When is insertion sort O(n)?
faq.a: When the array is already sorted or nearly so. For each element the while loop tests a[j] > key once, finds it false, and exits immediately — so the total is n-1 comparisons and zero shifts. More generally the running time is proportional to the number of inversions in the input.

faq.q: Is insertion sort stable?
faq.a: Yes, provided the shift condition is a strict a[j] > key. Elements equal to the one being inserted are never shifted, so the new element settles after its equals and relative order is preserved. Using >= breaks this.

title: How Merge Sort Works — Split, Sort, Merge, Visualized
metaDescription: Watch merge sort recurse down and merge back up in real C++. See the call stack build, the merge step in detail, and the bugs that silently drop elements.
intro: Merge sort is two ideas glued together: splitting a problem until it is trivial, and merging two sorted lists in one pass. The recursion is easy to accept and hard to picture, because nothing interesting happens on the way down — all the actual sorting occurs during the unwind, which is exactly the part a static diagram cannot show you.
code: void merge(vector<int>& a, int lo, int mid, int hi) {
for (int k = 0; k < (int)tmp.size(); k++) a[lo + k] = tmp[k];
void mergeSort(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi) {
codeNote: Top-down merge sort with inclusive bounds; merge builds the combined run in a temporary vector and copies it back over the original range.

howItWorks.heading: The descent does nothing but split
howItWorks.body: Every call halves its range and recurses. No comparison happens until a range shrinks to one element, at which point lo >= hi and the call returns immediately. Watching the call stack grow to depth log n before a single value moves is the moment merge sort clicks for most people.

howItWorks.heading: Merging is a two-finger scan
howItWorks.body: i walks the left half, j walks the right, and each step takes whichever front element is smaller. Because both halves are already sorted, the smaller of the two fronts is the smallest element remaining anywhere — that single fact makes the merge linear instead of quadratic.

howItWorks.heading: The drain loops handle the leftover
howItWorks.body: One half runs out first. The two trailing while loops copy whatever remains from the other half; it is already sorted and already larger than everything placed so far, so it can be appended wholesale.

howItWorks.heading: Copying back is what makes it in-place-ish
howItWorks.body: The merge builds its result in tmp and then overwrites a[lo..hi]. The array itself is always the source of truth, so the parent call sees a correctly sorted subrange without knowing anything about how it was produced.

howItWorks.heading: log n levels, n work per level
howItWorks.body: Halving reaches single elements after log2(n) levels. At every level the merges collectively touch each element exactly once. Multiply and you get n log n, and unlike quicksort there is no input that breaks it.

complexity.time: O(n log n) in all cases
complexity.note: The recursion depth is log n and each level merges every element once, with no dependence on input order; the O(n) space is the temporary buffer, which is the real cost and the reason quicksort is often preferred in memory-constrained code.

gotchas.title: Using lo > hi instead of lo >= hi as the base case
gotchas.body: With lo > hi, a single-element range keeps recursing: mid equals lo, the left call gets the identical range, and you get infinite recursion into a stack overflow. In DryRun the call stack shows the same (lo, hi) pair on frame after frame until it runs out of room, which is the whole diagnosis in one screen.

gotchas.title: Splitting into (lo, mid) and (mid, hi)
gotchas.body: The right half must start at mid + 1. Passing mid means the element at mid appears in both halves, so it gets duplicated and something else gets lost, and if the range has two elements the right call never shrinks and recursion never ends. The merge call must use the same mid the split used.

gotchas.title: Copying back to a[k] instead of a[lo + k]
gotchas.body: tmp is indexed from 0 but the range starts at lo. Writing a[k] = tmp[k] sorts the subrange into the front of the array instead of back where it came from, scrambling everything. It looks correct for the leftmost branch — which is the one people usually trace by hand — and wrong everywhere else.

gotchas.title: Using < instead of <= when comparing the two fronts
gotchas.body: if (a[i] < a[j]) takes from the right half when the values are equal, which reverses the original order of equal elements and makes the sort unstable. Merge sort's stability is the main reason to choose it over quicksort, and this one character throws it away.

faq.q: Why is merge sort O(n log n) in every case?
faq.a: Because the split is positional, not value-based: the range is always halved down the middle regardless of what the data contains. That fixes the recursion depth at log2(n), and each level does exactly n work merging. No input can unbalance it, which is the guarantee quicksort cannot make.

faq.q: Why does merge sort need extra memory?
faq.a: The merge step reads from two sorted runs and writes a combined run, and it cannot write into the array it is still reading without overwriting values it needs. The standard fix is an O(n) temporary buffer. In-place merge algorithms exist but are substantially slower and far more intricate.

faq.q: Is merge sort better than quick sort?
faq.a: It depends on what you need. Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) and is stable, which makes it the right choice for linked lists, external sorting, and when equal elements must keep their order. Quicksort is typically faster in practice on arrays because it sorts in place with better cache behaviour, at the cost of an O(n squared) worst case.

faq.q: Where does the actual sorting happen in merge sort?
faq.a: Entirely in the merge step, on the way back up the recursion. The downward phase only computes midpoints and makes calls — no element moves until a call returns and its parent merges two now-sorted halves. That is why the array looks completely untouched for the first log n steps of a trace.

title: Quick Sort Visualization — Partitioning, Pivots and the O(n²) Trap
metaDescription: Watch Lomuto partitioning move elements around the pivot in real C++, see the recursion split, and learn why sorted input makes quicksort quadratic.
intro: Quicksort does its work on the way down: pick a pivot, shove everything smaller to its left and everything larger to its right, and the pivot is permanently placed before you have sorted anything else. It is the fastest general-purpose sort in practice and the easiest to get catastrophically wrong, because a bad pivot choice silently turns n log n into n squared.
code: int partition(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi) {
for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) {
void quickSort(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi) {
codeNote: Lomuto partitioning with the last element as pivot — the simplest correct scheme, and the one whose worst case is easiest to trigger.

howItWorks.heading: The pivot ends up in its final position
howItWorks.body: After one partition call, every element left of index p is <= a[p] and everything right is >= it. That means a[p] is exactly where it belongs in the fully sorted array and is never touched again — which is why the recursive calls exclude it.

howItWorks.heading: i marks the boundary of the small region
howItWorks.body: During the scan, a[lo..i] holds values <= pivot and a[i+1..j-1] holds values > pivot. i starts at lo - 1 because the small region is initially empty. Every time j finds a small value, i advances and the two are swapped, growing the small region by one.

howItWorks.heading: The final swap seats the pivot
howItWorks.body: When the loop ends, i + 1 is the first slot of the large region. Swapping it with the pivot at hi drops the pivot exactly between the two regions and pushes a large value into the pivot slot, where it correctly belongs.

howItWorks.heading: Recursion sorts the two sides independently
howItWorks.body: Nothing ever crosses the pivot again, so the left and right subranges are fully independent problems. Unlike merge sort there is no combine step: when both calls return, the range is sorted.

howItWorks.heading: Balance is everything
howItWorks.body: If each partition splits roughly in half, the depth is log n and the total is n log n. If it splits into 0 and n-1 — which happens when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element — the depth is n and the total is n squared.

complexity.time: O(n log n) average, O(n squared) worst
complexity.note: Each partition is a linear scan, so the total cost is n times the recursion depth; depth is log n only when pivots land near the median, and picking the last element as pivot makes an already-sorted array hit the quadratic worst case every time.

gotchas.title: Sorted input is the worst case, not the best
gotchas.body: With a[hi] as the pivot, a sorted array always picks the maximum, producing an empty right side and an n-1 left side. Depth becomes n, the runtime becomes quadratic, and on a large array you get a stack overflow before you get an answer. The fix is median-of-three or a random pivot: swap a random index with hi before partitioning.

gotchas.title: Recursing on p instead of p - 1
gotchas.body: quickSort(a, lo, p) includes the pivot in the left subproblem. Since the pivot is already final, the range never shrinks when the pivot lands at hi, and you recurse forever on the same bounds. Watching the same lo and hi appear on consecutive stack frames identifies this in seconds.

gotchas.title: Using < instead of <= in the partition test
gotchas.body: if (a[j] < pivot) sends elements equal to the pivot into the large region. On an array where every value is identical, that puts all n-1 elements on one side and drives the same quadratic blowup — a genuinely common failure, since duplicate-heavy data is everywhere. Either keep <=, or switch to three-way partitioning.

gotchas.title: Initialising i to lo instead of lo - 1
gotchas.body: The small region starts empty, so the boundary must sit one slot before it. Starting at lo makes the first swap exchange an element with itself in the wrong place and shifts the whole partition by one, so the returned index is wrong and elements end up on the wrong side of the pivot.

faq.q: Why is quicksort O(n squared) in the worst case?
faq.a: Because a pivot that is the smallest or largest element splits the array into one empty side and one side of n-1 elements. The recursion then has depth n instead of log n, and each level still does a linear scan, giving n squared total. With last-element pivots, an already-sorted array triggers this on every single call.

faq.q: How do I avoid quicksort's worst case?
faq.a: Choose the pivot so an adversary or a sorted input cannot force it to the extreme. Median-of-three (first, middle, last) fixes sorted and reverse-sorted input cheaply; a randomly chosen pivot makes the quadratic case vanishingly unlikely for any fixed input. Production implementations also track recursion depth and switch to heapsort if it gets too deep.

faq.q: Is quicksort faster than merge sort?
faq.a: Usually yes on in-memory arrays, despite the worse asymptotic bound. Quicksort partitions in place with sequential memory access and no allocation, while merge sort copies through an O(n) buffer on every level. Merge sort wins when you need stability, guaranteed bounds, or you are sorting linked lists or data larger than memory.

faq.q: Is quicksort stable?
faq.a: No. Partitioning swaps elements across long distances, so two equal values can easily end up in the opposite of their original order. Making it stable requires extra space, at which point merge sort is the better choice.

title: Counting Sort Visualization — Sorting Without Comparing
metaDescription: See counting sort tally values and rebuild the array in real C++. Learn how the prefix-sum trick keeps it stable and when the value range makes it useless.
intro: Every comparison sort is stuck at n log n, but counting sort sidesteps the bound entirely by never comparing two elements. It uses values as array indices, which makes it linear — and also makes it completely unusable the moment your values are sparse or unbounded. Knowing exactly where that line sits is the useful part.
code: for (int v = 1; v <= maxVal; v++) count[v] += count[v - 1];
codeNote: The stable version: prefix sums turn counts into end positions, and walking the input backwards preserves the original order of equal keys.

howItWorks.heading: Values become indices
howItWorks.body: count[v] tallies how many times v appears. There is no comparison anywhere — the value itself selects the bucket, which is why the n log n lower bound does not apply. It is also why the value range, not just the element count, controls the cost.

howItWorks.heading: Prefix sums turn tallies into positions
howItWorks.body: After the second loop, count[v] holds the number of elements <= v, which is exactly one past the last index where v belongs in the output. That single transformation is what upgrades a bucket tally into a placement plan.

howItWorks.heading: Decrement then write
howItWorks.body: count[a[i]]-- moves the cursor from one-past-the-end to the actual slot, and that slot is then filled. The next element with the same value lands one position earlier, so equal values pack together from right to left.

howItWorks.heading: The backwards scan buys stability
howItWorks.body: Because slots fill right to left, processing the input from the end means the last equal element gets the rightmost slot and the first gets the leftmost. Iterate forwards instead and equal elements come out reversed.

howItWorks.heading: Cost is n plus k, not n log n
howItWorks.body: Two passes over n elements and two passes over the k+1 counters. When k is comparable to n this is genuinely linear; when k is a million and n is ten, you allocate a million counters to sort ten numbers.

complexity.time: O(n + k) where k is the value range
complexity.note: Linear only while k stays proportional to n — sorting values up to 10^9 needs a 10^9-entry counter array, so the algorithm degrades from fastest-available to unrunnable as the range grows, regardless of how few elements you have.

gotchas.title: Sizing the count array to maxVal instead of maxVal + 1
gotchas.body: count needs a slot for every value from 0 through maxVal inclusive. Off by one and the largest element writes past the end of the vector — undefined behaviour that frequently appears to work until the largest value shows up in your input.

gotchas.title: Negative values crash it
gotchas.body: count[a[i]]++ with a[i] = -3 indexes before the start of the vector. Counting sort assumes non-negative keys; for signed data, offset every value by -minVal on the way in and add it back on the way out, and size the counter array to maxVal - minVal + 1.

gotchas.title: Iterating forwards and losing stability
gotchas.body: Running the placement loop from i = 0 upward still sorts correctly but reverses equal elements. That only matters when you are sorting records by one field — and it matters enormously there, because radix sort is built on stable counting sort passes and silently produces garbage if this loop runs the wrong way.

gotchas.title: Writing to out and then reading a[i] from the same array
gotchas.body: If you try to make it in-place by writing back into a, you overwrite input you have not read yet and elements start duplicating. Counting sort fundamentally needs a separate output array once you want stability; watching values get clobbered mid-loop is the quickest way to see why.

faq.q: How can counting sort be faster than O(n log n)?
faq.a: The n log n lower bound applies only to sorts that determine order by comparing elements to each other. Counting sort never compares anything — it uses each value directly as an array index, extracting more information per operation than a yes/no comparison can. That extra power costs memory proportional to the value range.

faq.q: When should I not use counting sort?
faq.a: When the range of values is much larger than the number of elements. Sorting 100 integers that can each be up to a billion requires a billion-entry counter array, which is far worse than just calling a comparison sort. The rule of thumb is that k should be O(n) or smaller.

faq.q: Why does counting sort iterate the input backwards?
faq.a: To keep it stable. The prefix sums give each value the index just past its last output slot, and each placement decrements that cursor, so slots for a given value fill from right to left. Walking the input from the end means the last occurrence claims the rightmost slot, preserving the original relative order of equal elements.

faq.q: Can counting sort handle negative numbers?
faq.a: Not directly, since it uses values as array indices. Shift the data by subtracting the minimum value before counting and add it back when writing the output, sizing the counter array to maxVal - minVal + 1.

title: Two Pointers Technique — Visualized on Real Running Code
metaDescription: Watch two pointers converge on a sorted array in real C++. Learn why the technique is O(n) not O(n²), and the termination bugs that make it miss answers.
intro: Two indices walking toward each other can replace a nested loop, turning quadratic brute force into a single linear pass. The trick is not the two variables — it is the argument for why moving one of them is safe, which is where most people's intuition quietly breaks and where the wrong answers come from.
codeNote: Finds indices of two values in a sorted array that sum to the target — here 4 and 11, at indices 2 and 4.

howItWorks.heading: Sortedness is what makes a move safe
howItWorks.body: If a[lo] + a[hi] is too small, then a[lo] paired with anything smaller than a[hi] is also too small — so a[lo] cannot be part of any solution and can be discarded entirely. That elimination argument is the whole technique; without sorted input it collapses.

howItWorks.heading: Every step removes a candidate permanently
howItWorks.body: Each iteration either finds the answer or rules out one endpoint forever. Since there are n endpoints, the loop runs at most n times. Compare that to the nested loop, which re-examines pairs that were already eliminated.

howItWorks.heading: The pointers never cross
howItWorks.body: lo < hi keeps them distinct, so an element is never paired with itself. If you need to allow that, the condition becomes lo <= hi — but for a sum-of-two-distinct-elements problem, allowing it produces wrong answers on inputs like target = 2 * a[i].

howItWorks.heading: The search space is a rectangle you shrink
howItWorks.body: Think of all pairs (i, j) as a grid. Incrementing lo deletes a whole row; decrementing hi deletes a whole column. The pointers trace a staircase through the grid that visits O(n) cells instead of all n squared.

howItWorks.heading: The same-direction variant
howItWorks.body: Not all two-pointer problems converge. Removing duplicates in place, or partitioning by a predicate, uses a slow write pointer and a fast read pointer moving the same way. The shared idea is that one index describes the answer built so far and the other scans ahead.

complexity.time: O(n) for the scan, O(n log n) if you must sort first
complexity.note: Each iteration advances one pointer and neither ever moves backwards, so at most n iterations occur; the sort dominates when the input is not already ordered, which is why the technique shines on data that arrives sorted.

gotchas.title: Using while (lo <= hi) for distinct pairs
gotchas.body: When lo == hi, the code computes a[lo] + a[lo] and can report a pair made of a single element used twice. On input {1, 3, 7} with target 6 it wrongly returns index 1 twice. Use lo < hi unless the problem explicitly allows reuse.

gotchas.title: Forgetting to sort, or sorting a copy
gotchas.body: The technique is silently wrong on unsorted input — it returns not-found for pairs that exist, because the elimination logic is invalid. Equally common: sorting a local copy and then returning indices, which no longer correspond to the caller's array. If the problem wants original indices, sort (value, index) pairs or use a hash map instead.

gotchas.title: Moving both pointers on every iteration
gotchas.body: lo++; hi--; inside the loop body rather than in the branches skips pairs entirely. On {1, 2, 3, 4} with target 5 it checks 1+4, then 2+3 — fine — but on a six-element array it steps straight past valid combinations. Exactly one pointer moves per iteration.

gotchas.title: Handling duplicates by accident
gotchas.body: For problems that need all unique pairs rather than one, a naive loop emits the same pair repeatedly when the array has runs of equal values. After recording a match you must skip forward past the duplicates on both sides, not just advance by one. Watching lo and hi crawl through a run of identical values makes the missing skip obvious.

faq.q: When can I use the two pointers technique?
faq.a: When the array is sorted (or can be) and moving one pointer lets you rule out a whole set of candidates. The test is whether you can prove a statement like: if this pair's sum is too small, no pair involving the left element can work. If that inference holds, two pointers turns a nested loop into a single pass.

faq.q: Why is two pointers O(n) and not O(n squared)?
faq.a: Because neither pointer ever moves backwards. lo only increases and hi only decreases, so together they can move at most n times before meeting. Each move permanently eliminates one element from consideration, unlike a nested loop which revisits pairs it has already ruled out.

faq.q: What is the difference between two pointers and sliding window?
faq.a: A sliding window is a two-pointer variant where both pointers move in the same direction and the region between them is the answer under construction. Classic two pointers usually has the pointers converging from opposite ends, and the region between them is the part still to be searched.

faq.q: Does two pointers work on unsorted arrays?
faq.a: The converging variant does not — its correctness depends entirely on order. The same-direction variant does work on unsorted data for problems like in-place removal or partitioning, because those never rely on comparing across the gap.

title: Sliding Window Algorithm — Watch the Window Expand and Contract
metaDescription: See a sliding window grow and shrink over an array in running C++. Why the total work is O(n) despite the nested while, and the off-by-one traps.
intro: Recomputing a sum over every subarray is quadratic; updating one running total as a window slides is linear. The pattern looks like a nested loop but is not one, and understanding why the inner while does not multiply the cost is the difference between using this technique and merely recognising it.
codeNote: Finds the longest run of non-negative numbers whose sum stays at or below k, by expanding right and pulling left forward only when the sum overshoots.

howItWorks.heading: The window is the range [left, right]
howItWorks.body: right always advances by one per outer iteration; left only moves when the window becomes invalid. The invariant is that after the while loop, the window is the longest valid one ending at right.

howItWorks.heading: Incremental update replaces recomputation
howItWorks.body: Adding a[right] and subtracting a[left] keeps sum correct in O(1). The naive version recomputes the sum from scratch for every window, which is what makes it O(n squared). The entire speedup is this one substitution.

howItWorks.heading: The inner while is amortised, not nested
howItWorks.body: left never decreases and cannot exceed right, so across the whole run the while body executes at most n times total. Some outer iterations run it many times and most run it zero, but the sum over all iterations is bounded by n — that is why the algorithm is O(n) despite looking quadratic.

howItWorks.heading: Shrink until valid, then measure
howItWorks.body: The order matters: expand, restore the invariant, then record. Measuring before the while loop would count an invalid window; shrinking before adding a[right] would measure a window that is not maximal.

howItWorks.heading: Length is right - left + 1, always
howItWorks.body: Inclusive bounds on both ends mean the count includes both endpoints. A window where left == right has length 1, not 0 — the +1 is not decoration.

complexity.space: O(1) for sums, O(k) if the window needs a frequency map
complexity.note: Each index is added once by right and removed at most once by left, so the total pointer movement is bounded by 2n; the technique stops being valid the moment shrinking the window can no longer restore validity, which is what negative numbers do to a sum-based window.

gotchas.title: Negative numbers silently break the sum window
gotchas.body: The shrink loop assumes removing an element makes the sum smaller. With negative values that is false — dropping a -5 increases the sum, so the while loop can shrink the window to nothing and still not be valid, or terminate early and miss the answer. For arrays with negatives, use prefix sums with a map instead.

gotchas.title: Using if instead of while when shrinking
gotchas.body: One large element can invalidate the window by more than a single removal can fix. if (sum > k) removes exactly one element and moves on, leaving sum still over the limit, and every subsequent window is measured against a corrupt state. Put a large value in the middle of the array, step through in DryRun, and watch sum stay above k after the if has already run.

gotchas.title: Updating best before restoring the invariant
gotchas.body: Recording right - left + 1 above the while loop counts windows that violate the constraint, so the answer comes back too large. The measurement must be the last thing in the loop body.

gotchas.title: Forgetting to subtract when advancing left
gotchas.body: Writing left++ without sum -= a[left] leaves the running total describing a window that no longer exists. The result is usually a too-small answer that looks plausible on small inputs. Every pointer move must be paired with the matching state update — that pairing is the whole contract of the technique.

faq.q: Why is sliding window O(n) if it has a nested loop?
faq.a: Because the inner while loop is bounded globally, not per iteration. The left pointer only ever moves forward and can never pass right, so across the entire run it advances at most n times in total. The outer loop contributes n steps and the inner loop contributes at most n more, giving O(n) overall — this is amortised analysis, not worst-case-per-iteration.

faq.q: When should I use a sliding window?
faq.a: When the answer is a contiguous subarray or substring, and you can update the window's state in O(1) as elements enter and leave. It also needs a monotonic validity property: if a window is invalid, shrinking it from the left must be able to make it valid again. Sum-with-non-negative-values and character-frequency problems both satisfy this.

faq.q: What is the difference between fixed and variable sliding windows?
faq.a: A fixed window has a known size k, so left is always right - k + 1 and you add and remove one element per step with no inner loop. A variable window's size is determined by a constraint, so an inner while loop shrinks it until the constraint holds again. Fixed windows are simpler and strictly O(n) per step.

faq.q: Why does sliding window fail with negative numbers?
faq.a: Because the shrink step assumes removing an element reduces the sum. With negatives, removing an element can increase the sum, so the loop has no reliable way to restore validity and the window boundaries stop being meaningful. Prefix sums combined with a hash map handle those cases instead.

title: Prefix Sum Explained — Range Queries in O(1), Visualized
metaDescription: Build a prefix sum array in real C++ and watch range queries collapse to one subtraction. Covers the off-by-one that makes every range query wrong.
intro: Answering thousands of range-sum queries by looping over each range is a quadratic waste. Precompute the running total once and every range collapses to a single subtraction — the same trade you make when you keep a running balance instead of re-adding every transaction. The idea takes a minute; the indexing takes longer.
codeNote: Uses a size n+1 prefix array with a leading zero, so a range query needs no special case for l = 0.

howItWorks.heading: pre[i] is the sum of the first i elements
howItWorks.body: Note it is the first i, not up to index i. pre[0] = 0 (sum of nothing), pre[1] = a[0], pre[3] = a[0]+a[1]+a[2]. Getting this definition precise up front is what prevents every downstream off-by-one.

howItWorks.heading: Building it is one pass
howItWorks.body: Each entry is the previous entry plus one new element, so the whole table costs O(n) and a single addition per element. There is no cleverness here; the cleverness is in what it enables.

howItWorks.heading: A range is a difference of two prefixes
howItWorks.body: The sum of a[l..r] equals everything up to r minus everything before l, which is pre[r+1] - pre[l]. The elements before l are counted in both terms and cancel exactly, leaving the window you asked for.

howItWorks.heading: The leading zero removes the edge case
howItWorks.body: With a size-n array where pre[i] includes a[i], the query for l = 0 has nothing to subtract and needs an if. The extra slot makes pre[0] = 0 a valid thing to subtract, so one formula covers every range including the whole array.

howItWorks.heading: It generalises past sums
howItWorks.body: Any operation with an inverse works: XOR prefixes answer range-XOR queries, and counts of a predicate answer how many elements in a range satisfy it. Min and max do not work, because you cannot undo a min — that is what segment trees are for.

complexity.time: O(n) to build, O(1) per query
complexity.note: You pay one linear pass up front to make every subsequent query constant time, which wins as soon as you have more than a handful of queries; it is the wrong trade if the array changes between queries, since any update invalidates every prefix after it.

gotchas.title: Writing pre[r] - pre[l] instead of pre[r + 1] - pre[l]
gotchas.body: This drops a[r] from every query. With the 1-indexed prefix convention, pre[r] is the sum of everything strictly before index r. The answer is always short by exactly one element, so single-element ranges return 0 and the bug looks like an unrelated logic error.

gotchas.title: Sizing the prefix array to n instead of n + 1
gotchas.body: The query for the full array reads pre[n], which does not exist. In C++ that is an out-of-bounds read that often returns whatever happens to sit in the vector's spare capacity — frequently 0, which makes the result look almost right.

gotchas.title: Integer overflow on large sums
gotchas.body: Individual elements can fit in an int while their total does not. Summing 100,000 values around a million overflows a 32-bit int and produces negative range sums. Use long long for the prefix array even when the input is int; the values, not the array size, decide this.

gotchas.title: Rebuilding after every update
gotchas.body: Prefix sums are for static data. If an element changes, every prefix from that index onward is stale, and rebuilding is O(n) per update — worse than just looping over the range. If updates and queries interleave, you need a Fenwick tree, not this.

faq.q: What is a prefix sum array used for?
faq.a: Answering repeated range-sum queries in constant time. After one O(n) precomputation, the sum of any subarray a[l..r] is a single subtraction, pre[r+1] - pre[l]. It also underpins solutions to subarray-sum-equals-k, equilibrium index, and difference-array range updates.

faq.q: Why is the prefix array one element longer than the input?
faq.a: The extra leading zero represents the sum of an empty prefix, which lets the query formula work when l is 0 with no special case. Without it you need an if-statement on every query, which is exactly the kind of branch that gets forgotten and produces wrong answers only at the array boundary.

faq.q: How do I get the sum from index l to r using a prefix sum?
faq.a: Use pre[r + 1] - pre[l] with the leading-zero convention, where pre[i] is the sum of the first i elements. The subtraction cancels everything before l, leaving exactly a[l] through a[r] inclusive. If your prefix array has no leading zero, the formula becomes pre[r] - pre[l-1] with a special case for l = 0.

faq.q: Can prefix sums handle range minimum queries?
faq.a: No. The technique requires an invertible operation so the unwanted portion can be subtracted out, and minimum has no inverse — knowing the min of the first r elements and the min of the first l tells you nothing about the min in between. Use a sparse table or segment tree for that.

title: Kadane's Algorithm — Maximum Subarray Sum, Step by Step
metaDescription: Watch Kadane's algorithm decide between extending and restarting on every element, in real C++. Includes the all-negative bug almost everyone writes first.
intro: The maximum subarray problem looks like it needs to consider every start and end pair, and it does not. Kadane's insight is that at each position you face exactly one decision — extend the run you are on, or abandon it and start fresh — and the answer to that question only depends on whether the run so far is helping.
code: if (cur + a[i] > a[i]) cur = cur + a[i];
codeNote: Initialises from a[0] rather than 0, so the all-negative case correctly returns the largest single element (-2 here) instead of 0.

howItWorks.heading: cur is the best subarray ending exactly here
howItWorks.body: Not the best anywhere — the best that finishes at index i. Pinning the definition to end at i is what makes the recurrence work, because a subarray ending at i either includes i-1's run or consists of a[i] alone.

howItWorks.heading: The decision is extend or restart
howItWorks.body: cur + a[i] versus a[i] compares continuing the previous run against starting over at i. Continuing wins exactly when cur > 0. A negative running total is dead weight: whatever comes next is better off without it.

howItWorks.heading: best is a separate running maximum
howItWorks.body: cur can and should drop when the array turns negative. best remembers the highest cur ever seen, so a strong early run is not lost when a later stretch of negatives drags cur down.

howItWorks.heading: One pass, no lookahead
howItWorks.body: The decision at i needs only cur from i-1 and the value a[i]. Nothing about the future is required, which is why a single left-to-right scan suffices and why this is a textbook example of dynamic programming with O(1) state.

howItWorks.heading: Recovering the indices
howItWorks.body: If you need where the maximum subarray is and not just its sum, track a tentative start that resets whenever cur restarts, and commit it to the answer whenever best updates. Adding this after the fact is where most implementations go wrong, because the start must be recorded at restart time, not at update time.

complexity.note: One comparison and one addition per element, with only two integers of state; the brute force is O(n squared) or O(n cubed) because it re-sums ranges that Kadane collapses into a single carried value.

gotchas.title: Initialising best and cur to 0
gotchas.body: int best = 0 returns 0 for an all-negative array, implicitly claiming the empty subarray is a valid answer. Most problem statements require a non-empty subarray, where the correct answer is the largest single element. Initialise both from a[0] and start the loop at i = 1.

gotchas.title: Updating best inside the else branch
gotchas.body: Putting the best check only on the extend path misses the case where a single large positive element restarts the run and is itself the maximum. On {-10, 7, -10} you would return -10. The best update belongs after the if/else, unconditionally.

gotchas.title: Resetting cur to 0 instead of a[i]
gotchas.body: The common if (cur < 0) cur = 0; variant works only if you add a[i] before the check, not after. Mixing the two orderings gives a cur that lags one element behind the window it claims to describe — stepping through and comparing cur against the subarray it is supposed to represent exposes the mismatch immediately.

gotchas.title: Reading a[0] from an empty vector
gotchas.body: The initialisation dereferences a[0] before any bounds check. An empty input is undefined behaviour rather than a clean error. If empty input is possible, return a sentinel or throw before touching the array.

faq.q: How does Kadane's algorithm work?
faq.a: It scans the array once, keeping the best sum of a subarray that ends at the current position. At each element it chooses between extending the previous run or starting a new run at that element, whichever is larger, and separately tracks the highest value that quantity has ever reached. That highest value is the maximum subarray sum.

faq.q: Why does Kadane's algorithm fail on all-negative arrays?
faq.a: It does not fail if initialised correctly — it fails when best and cur start at 0, because 0 then represents an empty subarray that beats every real one. Initialising both to a[0] and looping from index 1 makes it return the largest single element, which is the correct non-empty answer.

faq.q: Is Kadane's algorithm dynamic programming?
faq.a: Yes. The recurrence is cur[i] = max(a[i], cur[i-1] + a[i]), a classic optimal-substructure formulation. Because each state depends only on the immediately previous one, the DP table collapses to a single variable, which is why it looks like a simple loop rather than typical DP.

faq.q: How do I find the actual subarray, not just the sum?
faq.a: Keep a tentative start index that resets to i whenever the algorithm restarts the run, and record start and end into the answer only when best is updated. The critical detail is that the tentative start must be set at the moment of the restart, before you know whether that run will win.

title: Two Sum — The Hash Map Trick, Visualized
metaDescription: Why Two Sum is O(n) with a hash map and O(n squared) without, on real C++. Includes the insert-before-lookup bug that pairs an element with itself.
intro: Two Sum is the first problem where most people meet the core trick of algorithmic thinking: instead of searching for a partner, remember what you have seen so you can be found. That inversion — from asking to being asked — is what collapses the nested loop, and it reappears in half of the problems you will solve afterwards.
codeNote: Single pass: it looks for the complement among values already stored, then records the current value — order matters and is the source of the classic bug.

howItWorks.heading: Turn the search around
howItWorks.body: The brute force asks, for each i, which later j completes the pair. The hash version asks, for each i, whether some earlier element was waiting for exactly this value. Both find the same pair; only one costs O(1) per element.

howItWorks.heading: The complement is fully determined
howItWorks.body: Given a[i] and the target, the partner must be target - a[i]. There is nothing to search for — you compute the exact value you need and ask the map whether it exists. That is why no comparison loop is required.

howItWorks.heading: Lookup before insert
howItWorks.body: Checking the map before adding a[i] guarantees the match came from a strictly earlier index. Insert first and a[i] can match itself whenever target is exactly 2 * a[i].

howItWorks.heading: The map stores value to index
howItWorks.body: The key is the value because that is what you look up; the payload is the index because that is what you must return. Getting these backwards is a surprisingly common mistake and produces a map you cannot query.

howItWorks.heading: Duplicates resolve themselves
howItWorks.body: If a value appears twice, the first occurrence is stored and the second finds it. The later assignment seen[a[i]] = i overwrites the earlier index, but only after any pair involving it would already have been found.

complexity.note: Each element does one hash lookup and one insert, both expected O(1), so the pass is linear; worst-case hashing degrades to O(n) per operation with adversarial keys, and the O(n) space is the price you pay to avoid the quadratic scan.

gotchas.title: Inserting before looking up
gotchas.body: If seen[a[i]] = i comes first, then for target 6 and input {3, 2, 4} the element 3 finds itself and you return {0, 0}. The lookup must happen against the map as it was before the current element was added.

gotchas.title: Sorting to use two pointers, then returning wrong indices
gotchas.body: The two-pointer approach requires sorted input, but sorting destroys the original positions, so the indices you return refer to the sorted copy. If the problem wants original indices, either use the hash map or sort pairs of (value, index) and return the stored index.

gotchas.title: Using seen[need] to test membership
gotchas.body: operator[] on an unordered_map inserts a default-constructed 0 when the key is missing. Writing if (seen[need]) both mutates the map and misreads a genuine index 0 as absent. Use count() or find(), not the subscript, for existence checks. The map quietly gaining an entry on every miss is obvious the moment you watch its contents step by step in DryRun, and invisible in the final output.

gotchas.title: Assuming exactly one solution exists
gotchas.body: The classic problem statement promises a unique answer, and the early return depends on it. If your input can have several valid pairs, this returns whichever comes first in scan order, which is not necessarily the one your tests expect.

faq.q: Why is the hash map solution to Two Sum O(n)?
faq.a: Because each element is processed once and each processing step does a constant-time hash lookup and insert. The brute force is O(n squared) because for every element it scans the rest of the array; the hash map replaces that scan with a single direct lookup of the exact complement value.

faq.q: Can Two Sum be solved without extra space?
faq.a: Yes, by sorting the array and using two pointers converging from both ends, which uses O(1) extra space but O(n log n) time. The catch is that sorting changes the indices, so this only works when the problem asks for the values or when you sort value-index pairs together.

faq.q: Why check the hash map before inserting the current element?
faq.a: To prevent an element from pairing with itself. If you insert first, then for a target equal to twice the current value the lookup finds the entry you just wrote and returns the same index twice. Checking first guarantees any match came from a strictly earlier position.

faq.q: What if the array contains duplicate values?
faq.a: It still works. The first occurrence is stored in the map, and when the second occurrence computes its complement it finds that stored index. Overwriting the map entry afterwards is harmless because any pair involving the earlier index would already have been returned.

title: Rotate an Array — The Reversal Trick, Visualized
metaDescription: Rotate an array in place with three reversals, running as real C++. See why the trick works, and why forgetting k modulo n breaks it on large shifts.
intro: Shifting every element k positions with a temporary array is obvious and costs O(n) memory. Doing it in place with three reversals costs nothing extra and looks like a magic trick until you see the two halves swap position — at which point it becomes the kind of thing you never forget.
code: void reverseRange(vector<int>& a, int i, int j) {
codeNote: Rotates right by k using three in-place reversals; on {1..7} with k = 3 the result is 5 6 7 1 2 3 4.

howItWorks.heading: A right rotation is a block swap
howItWorks.body: Rotating right by k means the last k elements move to the front and the first n-k move behind them. Written as blocks, [A][B] becomes [B][A]. Every rotation algorithm is some way of performing that swap without a buffer.

howItWorks.heading: Reversing the whole array gets the blocks in the right order
howItWorks.body: Reversing [A][B] gives [reverse(B)][reverse(A)]. The blocks are now in the correct positions — B before A — but each one is internally backwards. That is the only insight the trick needs.

howItWorks.heading: Two more reversals fix the interiors
howItWorks.body: Reversing the first k elements restores B, and reversing the remaining n-k restores A. Three reversals, each linear, and no extra storage.

howItWorks.heading: k must be reduced modulo n
howItWorks.body: Rotating by n is the identity, so rotating by k and by k % n are the same operation. Without the modulo, k > n makes reverseRange receive indices outside the array.

howItWorks.heading: Total work is 2n swaps
howItWorks.body: The full reversal touches n elements and the two partial reversals touch n between them, so about n swaps in total — twice the memory traffic of the buffer version, but with O(1) space. That trade is usually worth it and occasionally is not.

complexity.note: Three passes that collectively reverse 2n positions, all in place; the alternative juggling algorithm using GCD cycles does exactly n moves instead of 2n but has far worse cache behaviour, which is why the reversal version is usually faster in practice.

gotchas.title: Forgetting k = k % n
gotchas.body: Rotating a 7-element array by 10 without the modulo calls reverseRange(a, 0, 9), which reads and writes three elements past the end. The array often survives it because vectors over-allocate, so the bug shows up as corrupted data much later rather than as a crash.

gotchas.title: Doing the modulo after taking n from an empty vector
gotchas.body: k % n divides by zero when the array is empty. The guard for n == 0 has to come before the modulo, not after. This is the one input nobody tests and the one that takes the process down.

gotchas.title: Confusing rotate-right with rotate-left
gotchas.body: The same three reversals with k replaced by n - k rotate the other direction. If your output looks correct but shifted the wrong way, you have the direction convention inverted, not a bug in the reversals. Check against a small example by hand before touching the code.

gotchas.title: Reversing with i <= j instead of i < j
gotchas.body: When the range has odd length, i == j at the midpoint and the element is swapped with itself — harmless. But if you then also decrement and increment past each other, an off-by-one in a hand-rolled loop can swap the same pair twice and undo the reversal. Watching the two indices cross makes it obvious whether the loop stopped at the right moment.

faq.q: How do you rotate an array in place?
faq.a: Reverse the entire array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n-k. The first reversal puts the two blocks in the correct order but internally backwards; the two partial reversals repair them. It uses O(1) extra space and O(n) time.

faq.q: Why do three reversals rotate an array?
faq.a: Because reversing a concatenation [A][B] produces [reverse(B)][reverse(A)] — the blocks swap places as a side effect. Since a right rotation by k is exactly the transformation from [A][B] to [B][A], you only need to undo the two internal reversals afterwards.

faq.q: What happens if k is larger than the array length?
faq.a: Rotating by n returns the array to its original state, so only k modulo n matters. Without reducing k first, the partial reversals get index bounds outside the array and read or write out of range, which in C++ is undefined behaviour rather than a clean error.

faq.q: Is the reversal method faster than using a temporary array?
faq.a: Not usually in raw speed — the buffer version does n reads and n writes, while the reversal version does about 2n swaps. The reversal method wins on memory: it needs no allocation at all, which matters for large arrays or constrained environments.

title: Reverse a Linked List — Watch the Pointers Flip
metaDescription: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively in real C++ and watch prev, cur and next move node by node. Includes the lost-pointer bug that truncates the list.
intro: Three pointers, four lines, and an ordering that is unforgiving: get the sequence wrong and you either lose the rest of the list or build a node that points at itself. This is the canonical pointer-manipulation exercise precisely because the code is short enough to hold in your head and still easy to get wrong.
code: while (r != NULL) { cout << r->val << ' '; r = r->next; }
codeNote: Builds 1 to 5 by prepending, then reverses it iteratively; the loop in main prints 5 4 3 2 1.

howItWorks.heading: prev is the reversed part, cur is the rest
howItWorks.body: At every point the list has been cut in two: everything behind cur already points backwards and is rooted at prev, and everything from cur onward still points forwards. The loop moves one node across that boundary per iteration.

howItWorks.heading: Save next before you destroy it
howItWorks.body: cur->next = prev overwrites the only reference to the remainder of the list. nxt must be captured first, otherwise the rest of the list is unreachable and leaked the instant you reassign the pointer.

howItWorks.heading: The four lines are a rotation
howItWorks.body: Read them as: remember where we were going, turn the current arrow around, advance the reversed head, advance the cursor. Every line depends on the one before it, which is why reordering any pair breaks it.

howItWorks.heading: prev starts as NULL for a reason
howItWorks.body: The original head becomes the new tail, and a tail must point to NULL. Initialising prev to NULL makes the first iteration set that terminator automatically with no special case.

howItWorks.heading: Return prev, not head
howItWorks.body: When the loop exits, cur is NULL and prev holds the last node processed — the original tail, which is now the head. head still points at the original first node, which is now the tail, so returning it gives you a one-element list.

complexity.note: Each node is visited exactly once and only three pointer variables are ever live; the recursive version has the same time complexity but uses O(n) stack space and will overflow on a list of a few hundred thousand nodes.

gotchas.title: Reassigning cur->next before saving cur->next
gotchas.body: Writing cur->next = prev first and then Node* nxt = cur->next captures prev instead of the real successor. The loop then bounces between two nodes forever or terminates immediately with a two-element list. DryRun draws the nodes and their arrows, so you see cur->next flip to prev and the entire tail simply detach.

gotchas.title: Returning head instead of prev
gotchas.body: The reversal is correct but you hand back a pointer to what is now the last node, so the caller sees a list of length one. The function compiles, runs, and returns a plausible-looking result, which makes this the most commonly shipped version of the bug.

gotchas.title: Creating a self-loop with prev = cur->next
gotchas.body: Any variant that sets a node's next to itself turns your traversal into an infinite loop. It usually comes from updating prev and cur in the wrong order, so that prev and cur refer to the same node when the assignment happens. If your print loop never ends, this is why.

gotchas.title: Recursing on a long list
gotchas.body: The elegant recursive reversal pushes one stack frame per node. At roughly 100,000 nodes you get a stack overflow — a crash with no useful message. Watching the call stack grow linearly makes the limit concrete in a way that the phrase O(n) space does not.

faq.q: How do you reverse a linked list?
faq.a: Walk the list with three pointers: prev (the reversed portion), cur (the node being moved), and a temporary holding cur->next. On each step, save cur->next, point cur->next at prev, then advance prev to cur and cur to the saved node. When cur reaches NULL, prev is the new head.

faq.q: Why do you need a temporary pointer to reverse a linked list?
faq.a: Because reversing a node's next pointer destroys the only reference to the rest of the list. Once cur->next is overwritten with prev, there is no way back to the remaining nodes. The temporary captures that successor before it is lost.

faq.q: Should I reverse a linked list iteratively or recursively?
faq.a: Iteratively, in almost every real situation. Both are O(n) time, but the iterative version uses O(1) space while the recursive version uses O(n) stack frames and will overflow on long lists. The recursive form is worth knowing as a teaching example, not as production code.

faq.q: What does the reverse function return?
faq.a: prev, which after the loop points at the last node processed — the original tail, now the head of the reversed list. Returning the original head is a common mistake and yields a single-node list, since that node's next was set to NULL on the first iteration.

title: Detect a Cycle in a Linked List — Floyd's Algorithm Visualized
metaDescription: Watch the fast and slow pointers chase each other in real C++ and see why they must meet inside a cycle. Includes the null check that crashes.
intro: A list with a cycle has no end, so any traversal that waits for NULL runs forever. Floyd's trick is to send a second pointer at double speed: if the track loops, the faster one laps the slower and they collide. It uses two pointers and no memory, which is why it beats the obvious hash-set approach.
code: a->next = b; b->next = c; c->next = b;
codeNote: Builds a three-node list whose tail points back to the second node, then detects the loop with two pointers and no extra memory.

howItWorks.heading: Two speeds on the same track
howItWorks.body: slow advances one node per iteration and fast advances two. On a finite list fast reaches NULL first and the loop ends. Inside a cycle neither can escape, so they keep circling.

howItWorks.heading: Why they must collide
howItWorks.body: Once both pointers are inside the cycle, the gap between them changes by exactly one node per iteration, because fast gains one net position per step.
