A gap that shrinks by one each step must eventually reach zero — it cannot jump over, which is the reason a step of two works and larger steps need more care.

howItWorks.heading: The loop condition guards two dereferences
howItWorks.body: fast->next->next reads through two pointers, so both fast and fast->next must be non-NULL before the step. Checking them in that order is what makes the condition safe, since && short-circuits.

howItWorks.heading: slow needs no null check
howItWorks.body: slow is always at or behind fast, so if fast is safe to advance, slow certainly is. That asymmetry is why only fast appears in the condition.

howItWorks.heading: Finding where the cycle starts
howItWorks.body: After a meeting, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet again at the cycle entrance. That follows from the distance arithmetic — the distance from the head to the entrance equals the distance from the meeting point to the entrance, modulo the cycle length.

complexity.note: The slow pointer travels at most the length of the list before the two meet inside the cycle, so the work is linear; the hash-set alternative is also O(n) time but costs O(n) memory to store every visited node.

gotchas.title: Checking fast->next->next in the condition
gotchas.body: while (fast != NULL && fast->next->next != NULL) dereferences fast->next before verifying it is non-NULL. On an even-length list without a cycle this segfaults on the final iteration. The condition must be fast != NULL && fast->next != NULL, with the double step inside the body.

gotchas.title: Comparing values instead of pointers
gotchas.body: if (slow->val == fast->val) reports a cycle whenever two distinct nodes happen to hold the same number. Cycle detection is about identity — compare the pointers themselves.

gotchas.title: Starting fast at head->next
gotchas.body: Some versions initialise slow = head and fast = head->next to make the pointers distinct before the loop. That works, but it crashes on an empty list and changes where the meeting point lands, which silently breaks the follow-up code that finds the cycle entrance. Keep both at head and check after advancing.

gotchas.title: Assuming the meeting point is the cycle start
gotchas.body: It almost never is. The pointers meet somewhere inside the loop determined by the entry offset, not at the entrance. Stepping through and watching where the two pointers coincide relative to the loop entry makes it clear why a second phase is needed.

faq.q: How does Floyd's cycle detection work?
faq.a: Two pointers traverse the list at different speeds — one node per step and two nodes per step. If the list ends, the fast pointer reaches NULL and there is no cycle. If there is a cycle, both pointers become trapped in it and the faster one closes the gap by exactly one node per iteration until they land on the same node.

faq.q: Why do the slow and fast pointers always meet in a cycle?
faq.a: Because once both are inside the loop, the distance from fast to slow decreases by exactly one node each iteration — fast moves two, slow moves one, netting one step of progress. A distance that decreases by one at a time must hit zero exactly; it cannot skip past, which guarantees a meeting within at most one cycle length.

faq.q: Can I detect a cycle with a hash set instead?
faq.a: Yes. Store every node pointer you visit and report a cycle the first time you see one twice. It is easier to reason about and also O(n) time, but it costs O(n) memory. Floyd's algorithm gets the same answer in constant space, which is why it is the standard.

faq.q: How do I find the node where the cycle begins?
faq.a: After the two pointers meet, move one of them back to the head and then advance both one node at a time. The node where they meet the second time is the start of the cycle. This follows from the fact that the head-to-entrance distance and the meeting-point-to-entrance distance are congruent modulo the cycle length.

title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists — The Dummy Node Trick
metaDescription: Merge two sorted linked lists in real C++ and see why a dummy head removes every edge case. Covers the leftover-tail bug that silently drops nodes.
intro: Interleaving two ordered lists is the same two-finger scan that powers merge sort, but on pointers instead of indices — and the pointer version has an extra annoyance: choosing the head. The dummy node is the standard answer, and it is worth understanding as a general technique rather than as a one-off trick.
code: if (a->val <= b->val) { tail->next = a; a = a->next; }
while (m != NULL) { cout << m->val << ' '; m = m->next; }
codeNote: Splices existing nodes into one list without allocating — the dummy lives on the stack purely to give tail somewhere to start.

howItWorks.heading: Nodes are relinked, not copied
howItWorks.body: The merge changes next pointers on the existing nodes rather than allocating new ones. That makes it O(1) space, and it also means both input lists are destroyed — the caller cannot use a or b afterwards.

howItWorks.heading: The dummy removes the first-node special case
howItWorks.body: Without it, the first append has to set head instead of tail->next, which means an if on every iteration or a block of setup code before the loop. The dummy gives tail a valid node to write through from the very first step.

howItWorks.heading: tail always points at the last node of the result
howItWorks.body: After each append, tail advances onto the node just added. Every new node is attached at tail->next, so the result grows at the end in O(1) with no traversal.

howItWorks.heading: One line finishes the leftovers
howItWorks.body: When the loop ends, one list is exhausted and the other is not. Because the remainder is already sorted and already greater than everything appended so far, it can be attached wholesale with a single pointer assignment — no loop required.

howItWorks.heading: <= keeps the merge stable
howItWorks.body: Taking from a when the values are equal preserves the relative order of equal elements across the two lists. This is the same detail that makes merge sort stable, and it is inherited directly from this step.

complexity.note: Each node from both lists is examined and relinked at most once, and the only extra storage is the dummy plus two pointers; a recursive formulation is equally fast but consumes a stack frame per node.

gotchas.title: Forgetting to attach the remaining list
gotchas.body: Dropping the tail->next = (a != NULL) ? a : b line leaves the merged list truncated at whatever the loop last appended, and tail->next still points into the middle of an input list — or worse, at uninitialised memory. Every node after the shorter list's end simply disappears from the output.

gotchas.title: Returning dummy.next after taking its address wrongly
gotchas.body: Returning &dummy hands back a pointer to a stack object that dies when the function returns, so the caller reads freed memory. The dummy is scaffolding; only dummy.next is a real result. If you allocate the dummy with new instead, remember to delete it.

gotchas.title: Not initialising dummy.next
gotchas.body: If both input lists are empty the loop never runs and the final assignment sets dummy.next to b, which is NULL — fine. But any variant that returns early before that line reads an uninitialised pointer. Setting dummy.next = NULL up front costs nothing and closes the hole.

gotchas.title: Advancing tail before setting tail->next
gotchas.body: Reversing those two lines makes tail run ahead of the node it was supposed to link, producing a list that skips elements or ends abruptly. Stepping through node by node and watching where tail sits after each append makes the ordering requirement obvious.

faq.q: Why use a dummy node when merging linked lists?
faq.a: It gives you a node to append to before the real head exists, so the loop body never needs a special case for the first element. Without it, every iteration would have to check whether the result list is still empty. At the end you return dummy.next and discard the dummy.

faq.q: Does merging two sorted lists need extra memory?
faq.a: No. The standard iterative merge only rewires the next pointers of the existing nodes, so it uses O(1) extra space regardless of list length. It does consume the input lists — after the call, the original head pointers no longer describe valid separate lists.

faq.q: Why compare with <= instead of < when merging?
faq.a: To keep the merge stable. When the two front values are equal, taking from the first list preserves the original relative order of equal elements. Using < takes from the second list instead and reverses them, which matters whenever the nodes carry payload beyond the sort key.

faq.q: How is this related to merge sort?
faq.a: It is exactly merge sort's combine step, expressed on pointers instead of array indices. Merge sort on a linked list uses this function directly: split the list in half, sort each half recursively, then merge. Because linked lists need no auxiliary array, merge sort is the natural choice for them.

title: Valid Parentheses — Why This Problem Needs a Stack
metaDescription: Check balanced brackets with a stack in real C++ and watch it push and pop. Learn why a counter is not enough and which edge cases break naive solutions.
intro: Counting openers and closers is enough for one bracket type and completely wrong for three. The moment you have to remember which kind of bracket you are inside, and in what order, you need a structure that gives back the most recent thing first — which is the clearest practical argument for a stack that exists.
codeNote: Uses a vector as the stack so every push and pop is visible as a plain array operation; prints 1 then 0.

howItWorks.heading: An opener is a promise
howItWorks.body: Pushing a bracket records an obligation to close it later. The stack holds every promise that is still outstanding, in the order they were made, with the most recent on top.

howItWorks.heading: A closer must match the most recent promise
howItWorks.body: Brackets nest, so the only bracket you are allowed to close is the innermost open one — the top of the stack. That single rule is what rejects ([)], where the closer does not match the most recent opener even though the counts are balanced.

howItWorks.heading: An empty stack on a closer is an immediate failure
howItWorks.body: A closing bracket with nothing outstanding means the string closes something that was never opened, as in ())(. Checking st.empty() before reading back() is both a correctness rule and a safety check against undefined behaviour.

howItWorks.heading: A non-empty stack at the end is also a failure
howItWorks.body: Leftover entries mean promises that were never kept, as in ((. Returning st.empty() rather than plain true is what catches this, and it is the check most people forget.

howItWorks.heading: Why a counter is not sufficient
howItWorks.body: A counter tracks how many brackets are open but not which ones. It accepts ([)] because the total rises and falls correctly. Only for a single bracket type do a counter and a stack agree — and even then the counter must be checked for going negative.

complexity.note: Each character is pushed and popped at most once; the worst case for memory is a string of all openers such as ((((((, which stores every character before discovering the failure at the end.

gotchas.title: Returning true instead of st.empty()
gotchas.body: The loop only detects mismatches and unexpected closers. A string like ({[ passes every in-loop check and leaves three unmatched openers behind. Ending with return true accepts it. This is the single most common bug in this problem.

gotchas.title: Reading back() without checking empty()
gotchas.body: Calling back() or pop_back() on an empty vector is undefined behaviour, not an exception. On input )( it often returns garbage that happens not to match, so the function accidentally returns the right answer — until the day it does not.

gotchas.title: Using a counter for multiple bracket types
gotchas.body: A single integer incremented on openers and decremented on closers accepts ([)] and [{]}. It cannot distinguish types by construction. If your solution passes the simple tests and fails the interleaved ones, this is why.

gotchas.title: Assuming the input contains only brackets
gotchas.body: If the string can hold other characters, the else branch treats every letter as a closing bracket and immediately fails. Either filter non-bracket characters explicitly or restructure the branch to test for known closers rather than using else as a catch-all.

faq.q: Why does valid parentheses need a stack?
faq.a: Because brackets nest, and the only bracket a closer may match is the most recently opened one that is still unclosed. A stack returns exactly that element in O(1). A counter only tracks how many brackets are open, not which types or in what order, so it wrongly accepts strings like ([)].

faq.q: What is the time complexity of the valid parentheses algorithm?
faq.a: O(n) time and O(n) space. Every character is examined once and pushed or popped at most once. The space is worst-case n, reached by a string consisting entirely of opening brackets, all of which must be remembered until the end.

faq.q: Why check that the stack is empty at the end?
faq.a: Because leftover openers are unmatched. The loop can only detect a closer that mismatches or that arrives with nothing open — it has no way to notice that ((( never closed. Returning st.empty() rather than true is what makes those cases fail correctly.

faq.q: Can you solve valid parentheses without a stack?
faq.a: Only for a single bracket type, where one counter that never goes negative and ends at zero is equivalent. With multiple types you need to remember the sequence of open brackets, and any structure that does that is a stack, whether you call it one or implement it with an array and an index.

title: How a Stack Works — LIFO, Visualized on Real Memory
metaDescription: See push and pop change a stack in real running C++, why LIFO shows up everywhere from undo to recursion, and the empty-pop bug that returns garbage.
intro: A stack is defined entirely by one restriction: you may only touch the most recently added item. That sounds like a limitation and it is actually the point — the restriction is what makes stacks fast, simple, and the right model for anything with nesting, from bracket matching to the call frames your own program runs on.
codeNote: Implements the stack as a vector so every push and pop is a visible array operation rather than a black box.

howItWorks.heading: Only the top is reachable
howItWorks.body: push_back adds at the end, back reads the end, pop_back removes the end. There is no operation that reaches into the middle, and that is deliberate: the guarantee that access is restricted is what lets the structure be this simple.

howItWorks.heading: Everything is O(1) because nothing shifts
howItWorks.body: Adding and removing at the end of a vector touches one slot. Compare that to inserting at the front, which has to move every existing element. Stacks are fast because they only ever operate where no shifting is needed.

howItWorks.heading: LIFO models nesting
howItWorks.body: Anything that opens and closes in nested order — brackets, HTML tags, function calls, undo steps — matches the last-in-first-out discipline exactly. When you find yourself needing the most recent unfinished thing, you have found a stack.

howItWorks.heading: Growth is amortised, not free
howItWorks.body: A vector doubles its capacity when it fills, so an occasional push copies every element. Averaged over many pushes the cost is still O(1) per operation, but individual pushes can be slow — this matters if you are measuring latency rather than throughput.

howItWorks.heading: Your program already runs on one
howItWorks.body: Every function call pushes a frame holding parameters and locals; every return pops it. That is why a runaway recursion produces a stack overflow, and why local variables vanish when a function ends — the same LIFO rules, applied to memory.

complexity.time: O(1) for push, pop, top and empty
complexity.note: All operations touch a single position at the end of the underlying storage, so none of them depend on the number of elements; the only non-constant moment is a reallocation when a vector-backed stack outgrows its capacity.

gotchas.title: Calling back() or pop_back() on an empty stack
gotchas.body: Neither throws. back() on an empty vector is undefined behaviour and typically returns whatever bytes are sitting there, so your code proceeds with a plausible-looking garbage value. Always guard with !st.empty(), and be aware that std::stack behaves the same way.

gotchas.title: Expecting pop to return the value
gotchas.body: In C++, pop_back and stack::pop return void. Writing int x = st.pop_back(); does not compile, and the fix is to read back() first and then pop. This split exists for exception-safety reasons, and it trips up everyone arriving from Python or Java.

gotchas.title: Holding a reference across a push
gotchas.body: int& top = st.back(); followed by st.push_back(...) can invalidate top, because the push may reallocate the vector and move every element to new memory. The reference then points at freed storage. Copy the value instead of binding a reference if a push might follow.

gotchas.title: Using a stack when you needed a queue
gotchas.body: Draining a stack reverses the insertion order. If your breadth-first search visits nodes in the wrong sequence, or your task list processes the newest item first, you have picked the wrong structure — and the output is often subtly wrong rather than obviously broken.

faq.q: What does LIFO mean?
faq.a: Last In, First Out — the most recently added element is the first one removed. It describes a stack of plates: you take from the top, and the plate you put down last is the one you pick up first. The opposite discipline, FIFO, describes a queue.

faq.q: Why are stack operations O(1)?
faq.a: Because every operation acts on one end of the storage, so no other elements need to move. Push writes one slot, pop discards one slot, and top reads one slot — none of these depend on how many elements the stack holds. Inserting or removing anywhere else would require shifting.

faq.q: What is a stack used for in programming?
faq.a: Anywhere the most recent unfinished item is the one you need next: matching brackets, evaluating expressions, undo history, depth-first search, backtracking, and the function call stack itself. The common thread is nested structure — things that open and close in order.

faq.q: What is the difference between a stack and a queue?
faq.a: A stack removes the newest element (LIFO); a queue removes the oldest (FIFO). That single difference changes traversal order entirely — a graph search with a stack goes deep along one path, while the same search with a queue explores level by level.

title: How a Queue Works — FIFO and the Circular Buffer Trick
metaDescription: See a queue enqueue and dequeue in running C++, why a naive array queue is O(n), and how a circular buffer fixes it. Includes the full-vs-empty ambiguity.
intro: A queue serves the oldest waiting item first, which is the obvious fair policy and a surprisingly awkward thing to implement on an array. Removing from the front either shifts everything or leaves a hole, and the standard fix — wrapping the indices around — introduces an ambiguity that has its own well-known solution.
codeNote: A circular buffer of capacity 5: head plus count locates the write slot, and both indices wrap with modulo so no element is ever shifted.

howItWorks.heading: FIFO means two ends, not one
howItWorks.body: Items enter at the tail and leave at the head, so unlike a stack a queue must track both ends. Every implementation detail follows from that: you need two indices, or a head index plus a count.

howItWorks.heading: The naive array queue is quadratic
howItWorks.body: Dequeuing by erasing element 0 shifts every remaining element left, costing O(n) per removal. Draining n items therefore costs O(n squared). Nothing about the queue abstraction requires that — it is purely an artefact of a bad layout.

howItWorks.heading: Wrapping reuses the vacated space
howItWorks.body: Instead of moving elements back, move the head forward and let the tail wrap around to the freed slots. The modulo turns a linear array into a ring, so both operations become O(1) with no shifting at all.

howItWorks.heading: count disambiguates full from empty
howItWorks.body: With only head and tail indices, head == tail means both empty and completely full — the ring gives no way to tell. Storing an explicit count resolves it; the alternative is to waste one slot so full and empty never coincide.

howItWorks.heading: Where you meet queues
howItWorks.body: Breadth-first search, task schedulers, print spoolers, and any producer-consumer buffer. The defining property is that arrival order is the service order, which is what makes a queue explore a graph level by level rather than diving down one branch.

complexity.time: O(1) for enqueue, dequeue and front
complexity.note: Both ends are located by arithmetic rather than by scanning, so no operation depends on the number of items; the naive erase-from-front implementation is O(n) per dequeue and is the usual reason a queue-based solution runs slower than expected.

gotchas.title: Using vector::erase(begin()) as dequeue
gotchas.body: It works and is O(n), because every remaining element shifts down one slot. In a BFS over 100,000 nodes this alone turns a linear traversal into a quadratic one. Use std::queue or std::deque, or a circular buffer — the abstraction is right, the implementation is not.

gotchas.title: head == tail meaning both full and empty
gotchas.body: In a two-index circular buffer with no count, a full ring and an empty ring look identical. Enqueuing into a full queue then silently overwrites the oldest element, and the bug presents as mysteriously missing data much later. Track count explicitly or deliberately leave one slot unused.

gotchas.title: Forgetting the modulo on one of the indices
gotchas.body: It is easy to wrap head and forget the tail, or vice versa. The queue works perfectly until the first wraparound, so the failure only appears after roughly capacity operations — long after the code looked correct. Stepping through the wraparound in DryRun and watching head and tail cross the boundary is the fastest way to catch it.

gotchas.title: Reading front() without checking empty()
gotchas.body: Like a stack, an empty std::queue does not throw on front() or pop(); it is undefined behaviour. In a BFS this happens when the loop condition and the pop are out of sync, and it typically yields a garbage node id that indexes out of your adjacency list.

faq.q: What does FIFO mean?
faq.a: First In, First Out — elements leave in the same order they arrived, like people waiting in line. It is the opposite of a stack's LIFO discipline. FIFO ordering is what makes a queue-based graph traversal visit nodes in order of increasing distance from the start.

faq.q: Why is a circular queue better than a normal array queue?
faq.a: Because dequeuing from a plain array means either shifting every element (O(n) per removal) or abandoning the freed slots until the array is exhausted. A circular buffer advances the head index and lets the tail wrap around into the reclaimed space, making both operations O(1) with fixed memory.

faq.q: How do you tell if a circular queue is full or empty?
faq.a: Keep an explicit element count, or leave one slot permanently unused. Without one of these, a full ring and an empty ring both have head == tail and are indistinguishable, so the queue will happily overwrite live data. The count approach uses all capacity; the sacrificed-slot approach avoids an extra variable.

faq.q: When should I use a queue instead of a stack?
faq.a: When the oldest pending item should be handled first. Breadth-first search needs a queue to visit nodes in distance order; using a stack turns it into a depth-first search that finds paths but not shortest ones. Schedulers and buffers also want FIFO, because it bounds how long any single item waits.

title: Next Greater Element — The Monotonic Stack, Visualized
metaDescription: Watch a monotonic stack solve next greater element in one O(n) pass of real C++. Why elements get popped, and why indices beat values.
h1: Next Greater Element with a Monotonic Stack
intro: For each element, find the first larger value to its right. The nested-loop version is obvious and quadratic; the stack version is linear and looks like sleight of hand until you notice what it is really doing — throwing away elements that can never be the answer to anything again.
codeNote: Stores indices, not values, so the answer can be written back to the correct position; unresolved elements keep their -1.

howItWorks.heading: The stack holds unanswered questions
howItWorks.body: Every index on the stack is an element still waiting for a larger value to appear. Once a[i] resolves it, the index leaves and never returns. The stack size is the number of open questions, not a window.

howItWorks.heading: It stays decreasing, and that is the invariant
howItWorks.body: Values referenced by the stack are strictly decreasing from bottom to top. When a[i] arrives, it pops everything smaller — and because the stack was decreasing, everything it can resolve sits contiguously on top. That is why one while loop suffices.

howItWorks.heading: A popped element is answered forever
howItWorks.body: a[i] is the first value to its right that exceeded it, by construction: any earlier candidate would have popped it sooner. So res is written exactly once per index and never revised.

howItWorks.heading: Why it is O(n), not O(n squared)
howItWorks.body: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total number of while-loop iterations across the whole run is bounded by n. The inner loop can be long on one step and empty on the next, but the sum is linear.

howItWorks.heading: Leftovers are genuine -1s
howItWorks.body: Anything still on the stack at the end never found a larger element to its right, so the pre-filled -1 is the correct answer. No cleanup pass is needed — the initialisation already handles it.

complexity.note: Amortised linear because every index enters and leaves the stack at most once; the space is worst-case n, hit by a strictly decreasing array where nothing is ever resolved until the end.

gotchas.title: Pushing values instead of indices
gotchas.body: If the stack holds a[i] rather than i, you know which value was resolved but not where to write the answer. Duplicate values make it unrecoverable. Store indices and dereference with a[st.back()] when you need the value.

gotchas.title: Using <= instead of < in the pop condition
gotchas.body: a[st.back()] <= a[i] pops equal elements, which answers next greater or equal rather than strictly greater. On {2, 2, 3} it reports 2 for the first element instead of 3. Which one is correct depends on the problem statement, and mixing them up is a silent off-by-one in semantics.

gotchas.title: Checking a[st.back()] before checking empty()
gotchas.body: Reversing the operands in the while condition calls back() on an empty vector, which is undefined behaviour rather than a crash. It usually reads garbage that happens to be large, so the loop exits and the code appears to work — until it does not.

gotchas.title: Assuming the stack is a sliding window
gotchas.body: The stack is not the recent k elements; it is a decreasing subsequence that can span the entire array. On strictly decreasing input it holds every index at once. If you sized a fixed buffer for it, watch it grow past your assumed bound on {9,8,7,6,...}.

faq.q: What is a monotonic stack?
faq.a: A stack whose contents are kept in sorted order — increasing or decreasing — by popping elements that would violate that order before each push. The pops are not overhead: each popped element is being resolved at exactly the right moment, which is what makes these algorithms linear.

faq.q: Why is next greater element O(n) with a stack?
faq.a: Because each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the entire run, so the total work in the inner while loop is bounded by n regardless of how it is distributed. The brute force is O(n squared) because it re-scans the same elements for every starting position.

faq.q: Why does the stack store indices instead of values?
faq.a: Because when an element is finally resolved you have to record the answer at its original position. A value alone does not tell you where it came from, and duplicate values make it impossible to guess. Keeping indices lets you read the value with a[st.back()] whenever you need it.

faq.q: What other problems use a monotonic stack?
faq.a: Largest rectangle in a histogram, trapping rain water, daily temperatures, and stock span — all of them ask for the nearest element on one side satisfying a comparison. If you can phrase the question as nearest smaller or larger to the left or right, a monotonic stack solves it in one pass.

title: Tree Traversals — Inorder, Preorder and Postorder Visualized
metaDescription: Watch preorder, inorder and postorder recursion unfold on a real binary tree in C++. One line moves and the entire output order changes — see exactly why.
intro: The three depth-first traversals are the same recursive walk with one statement in three different places. That is genuinely all that separates them, and it explains why inorder produces sorted output on a BST while postorder is the only safe way to delete a tree — the position of the visit determines what has already happened when you arrive.
code: n->val = v; n->left = NULL; n->right = NULL;
codeNote: Inorder on this tree prints 1 2 3 4 6; move the cout above the first recursive call for preorder, or below the second for postorder.

howItWorks.heading: The walk is always the same
howItWorks.body: Every traversal descends left, then right, then returns. The recursion visits each node exactly three times — on arrival, between the two children, and on departure. Which of those moments you print at is the entire choice.

howItWorks.heading: Preorder: act before you descend
howItWorks.body: Printing before both calls means a node is emitted before anything beneath it. That gives you the root first, which is what you want for copying a tree or serialising it — the parent must exist before its children can be attached.

howItWorks.heading: Inorder: act between the children
howItWorks.body: The left subtree is fully processed, then the node, then the right. On a binary search tree this yields values in sorted order for free, because everything left is smaller and everything right is larger, recursively.

howItWorks.heading: Postorder: act after you descend
howItWorks.body: Both subtrees are complete before the node is touched. That is the only correct order for freeing memory or computing a value that depends on both children's results, such as subtree size or height.

howItWorks.heading: The base case is where the depth is bounded
howItWorks.body: if (r == NULL) return; is what stops the recursion at the leaves. Every node's two null children each generate one call that immediately returns, so a tree of n nodes produces about 2n+1 calls in total.

complexity.space: O(h) where h is the height
complexity.note: Every node is visited a constant number of times, so time is linear regardless of shape; the space is the recursion stack, which is O(log n) for a balanced tree and O(n) for a degenerate one that has become a linked list.

gotchas.title: Missing or misplaced base case
gotchas.body: Without if (r == NULL) return;, the first leaf dereferences a null pointer and segfaults. Putting the check after the first recursive call is equally broken — the crash happens on the way down, before the guard is ever reached.

gotchas.title: Expecting inorder to be sorted on any tree
gotchas.body: Inorder produces sorted output only on a binary search tree. On an arbitrary binary tree it produces an order that reflects the shape, not the values. If your inorder output is not sorted, check whether the tree actually satisfies the BST property before suspecting the traversal.

gotchas.title: Freeing nodes in preorder
gotchas.body: delete r before recursing destroys the node whose left and right pointers you are about to read. It often appears to work because freed memory is not immediately overwritten, then crashes intermittently under load. Deletion must be postorder: free the children, then the parent.

gotchas.title: Deep recursion on a degenerate tree
gotchas.body: A tree built by inserting already-sorted values becomes a linked list of height n, and the traversal needs n stack frames. At a few hundred thousand nodes that overflows. Watching the call stack grow one frame per node makes the difference between a balanced and degenerate tree immediately visible.

faq.q: What is the difference between inorder, preorder and postorder traversal?
faq.a: They differ only in when the current node is processed relative to its children. Preorder handles the node before both subtrees, inorder between the left and right subtrees, and postorder after both. The traversal path through the tree is identical in all three; only the moment of the visit moves.

faq.q: Why does inorder traversal of a BST give sorted output?
faq.a: Because the BST property guarantees every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in the right is larger. Inorder emits the entire left subtree, then the node, then the entire right subtree — applied recursively, that is exactly ascending order.

faq.q: Which traversal should I use to delete a tree?
faq.a: Postorder. You must free both children before freeing the parent, because once the parent is deleted its left and right pointers are no longer valid to read. Preorder deletion reads through a freed pointer, which is undefined behaviour that often appears to work in testing.

faq.q: What is the space complexity of tree traversal?
faq.a: O(h), where h is the tree's height, because the recursion holds one stack frame per level on the current path. That is O(log n) for a balanced tree but O(n) for a degenerate one, which is why inserting sorted data into an unbalanced BST can turn a traversal into a stack overflow.

title: Binary Search Tree — Insert and Search, Visualized
metaDescription: Watch BST insertion and search descend a real tree in running C++. Learn why sorted input destroys performance and what actually makes a tree a valid BST.
intro: A binary search tree is binary search made structural: instead of computing a midpoint, the shape of the data decides where to go next. That works beautifully when the tree is bushy and collapses to a linked list when it is not, which is why every serious implementation adds rebalancing on top.
code: n->val = v; n->left = NULL; n->right = NULL;
else if (v > root->val) root->right = insert(root->right, v);
for (int i = 0; i < 7; i++) root = insert(root, vals[i]);
codeNote: Insert returns the (possibly new) subtree root, which is what lets the caller reattach it with root->left = insert(...) and handles the empty-tree case for free.

howItWorks.heading: The invariant is recursive, not local
howItWorks.body: Every value in a node's left subtree must be less than the node, and every value on the right greater — not just the immediate children, the entire subtree. This distinction is the source of the classic isValidBST bug and matters more than the definition suggests.

howItWorks.heading: Search is one comparison per level
howItWorks.body: At each node you compare and pick a side, discarding the other subtree entirely. That is the same halving idea as binary search, except the split point is wherever the tree happens to put it rather than the exact middle.

howItWorks.heading: Insertion always creates a leaf
howItWorks.body: The descent continues until it falls off the tree at a NULL, and the new node is attached there. No existing node ever moves, which makes insertion cheap but also means the tree's shape is entirely determined by insertion order.

howItWorks.heading: Returning the subtree root does the linking
howItWorks.body: Because insert returns a Node*, the parent reassigns root->left or root->right with the result. For an existing subtree that is a no-op reassignment; for an empty one it attaches the new node. One return value covers both cases without any parent-pointer bookkeeping.

howItWorks.heading: Height is the real complexity
howItWorks.body: Every operation costs O(h). Random insertion order gives h around log n; sorted insertion gives h equal to n. The gap between those two is the entire reason AVL and red-black trees exist.

complexity.time: O(h) per operation — O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate
complexity.space: O(h) for recursive insert, O(1) for iterative search
complexity.note: Cost tracks the tree's height rather than its size, and height depends entirely on insertion order; feeding a plain BST already-sorted data produces a chain where every operation is a linear scan.

gotchas.title: Validating a BST by comparing only with children
gotchas.body: Checking node->left->val < node->val at each node accepts invalid trees. A node with value 6 in the left subtree of a root of 5 passes every local check but violates the global ordering. Validation must carry a (min, max) range down the recursion, narrowing it at each step.

gotchas.title: Inserting sorted data
gotchas.body: Inserting 1,2,3,...,n gives every node only a right child — a linked list with extra pointers. Search becomes O(n) and any recursive traversal risks a stack overflow. Insert 1 through 10 in order in DryRun and watch the tree render as a single descending chain — the clearest possible demonstration of why balancing exists.

gotchas.title: Forgetting to reassign the result of insert
gotchas.body: Calling insert(root->left, v); without assigning back to root->left builds the new node correctly and then discards the pointer to it. The tree never grows past its first node, and every element you inserted is leaked.

gotchas.title: Not handling duplicate values
gotchas.body: This implementation silently ignores duplicates because neither the < nor the > branch fires. That may be what you want, but if you expected a count or a second copy, elements will vanish with no error. Decide explicitly: ignore, keep a count in the node, or send equals consistently to one side.

faq.q: What makes a binary tree a binary search tree?
faq.a: Every node's entire left subtree contains only smaller values and its entire right subtree only larger ones, applied recursively at every node. The word entire is the important part — checking only the immediate children is not sufficient and accepts trees that break the ordering.

faq.q: Why is BST search O(log n) only sometimes?
faq.a: Because search cost equals the tree's height, and height depends on insertion order. Randomly ordered inserts produce a roughly balanced tree with height around log n, but sorted inserts produce a single chain of height n, making every search a linear scan. Self-balancing trees like AVL and red-black guarantee log n height regardless of input.

faq.q: What happens if you insert sorted data into a BST?
faq.a: You get a degenerate tree — effectively a linked list, since each new value is larger than everything before it and always goes right. All operations degrade to O(n), and recursive traversals can overflow the call stack on large inputs. This is the single most common way a BST-based solution becomes unusably slow.

faq.q: How do you find the minimum value in a BST?
faq.a: Follow left pointers from the root until a node has no left child; that node holds the minimum. The BST property guarantees nothing smaller exists anywhere else in the tree. The maximum is the mirror image — keep going right.

title: Height of a Binary Tree — Recursion That Returns Values
metaDescription: Compute tree height recursively in real C++ and watch the values propagate back up the call stack. Covers the off-by-one between height and node count.
h1: Computing the Height of a Binary Tree
intro: Most tree recursion prints things on the way down. Height computation is the first one where the answer flows back up: each call waits for both children to report, combines their results, and returns something to its own parent. Watching those return values propagate is what turns tree recursion from a memorised pattern into something you can reason about.
code: n->val = v; n->left = NULL; n->right = NULL;
codeNote: Returns -1 for an empty tree so height counts edges; this tree has height 3, along the path 1 to 2 to 4 to 5.

howItWorks.heading: Each node asks its children first
howItWorks.body: The two recursive calls run to completion before the return statement executes. A node cannot know its height until both subtrees have reported theirs, which is why nothing is computed on the way down.

howItWorks.heading: The answer is built during the unwind
howItWorks.body: Leaves return first, then their parents combine and return, and so on up to the root. Stepping through and watching each frame's lh and rh get filled in as its children return is the clearest possible picture of what a return value actually does.

howItWorks.heading: Max, not sum
howItWorks.body: Height is the longest single path, so you take the larger of the two subtree heights, not their total. Using + instead of max computes the total number of edges in the tree, which is a real quantity but a different one.

howItWorks.heading: The +1 accounts for the edge to the child
howItWorks.body: Standing at a node, the path down is one edge plus the longest path from the taller child. That single edge is where the +1 comes from, and it is what makes the recursion accumulate depth.

howItWorks.heading: The base case defines the convention
howItWorks.body: Returning -1 for NULL makes a single leaf have height 0, counting edges. Returning 0 for NULL makes a leaf have height 1, counting nodes. Neither is wrong, but mixing them within one codebase produces answers that are consistently off by one.

complexity.note: Every node is visited exactly once and does constant work, so time is linear in node count; the space is the recursion stack, which equals the height — meaning the very degenerate trees whose height you are measuring are also the ones most likely to overflow the stack while measuring it.

gotchas.title: Returning 0 for NULL and then reporting edge counts
gotchas.body: The two conventions differ by exactly one, and the mismatch propagates silently. A balance check that compares subtree heights still works either way, but any code that turns height into an index, a level number, or an array size will be off by one everywhere. Pick a convention and write it down.

gotchas.title: Adding instead of taking the maximum
gotchas.body: return 1 + lh + rh counts edges in the whole subtree rather than along the longest path. On a balanced tree it grows linearly with n instead of logarithmically, so the number looks wildly wrong — but on a chain-shaped tree it is accidentally correct, which is exactly the test case people try first.

gotchas.title: Calling height inside a balance check at every node
gotchas.body: The naive isBalanced computes height(node->left) and height(node->right) at every node, recomputing the same subtree heights repeatedly for O(n squared) total work. The fix is a single postorder pass that returns height and propagates a failure sentinel. On a deep tree the difference is dramatic and easy to observe in a step count.

gotchas.title: Stack overflow while measuring a degenerate tree
gotchas.body: A tree of 200,000 nodes inserted in sorted order is a chain, and the recursion needs 200,000 frames. The function that tells you the tree is unbalanced crashes because the tree is unbalanced. An explicit stack or a level-order count avoids it.

faq.q: What is the difference between height and depth of a tree?
faq.a: Height is measured upward from a node to its deepest descendant; depth is measured downward from the root to that node. The root has depth 0 and the maximum height; a leaf has height 0 and its depth equals its level. The height of the tree is the height of the root.

faq.q: Why does the height function return -1 for an empty tree?
faq.a: Because that convention counts edges rather than nodes, which makes a single-node tree have height 0. With the +1 in the return, a leaf's two null children both report -1 and the leaf correctly reports 0. Returning 0 for NULL is the node-counting convention and shifts every answer by one.

faq.q: How do you compute the height of a binary tree?
faq.a: Recursively: the height of a node is one plus the greater of its two subtree heights, with an empty subtree returning -1. Each node waits for both children to return before computing its own value, so the answer is assembled bottom-up during the recursion's unwind. It runs in O(n) time.

faq.q: Can you compute tree height without recursion?
faq.a: Yes, with a level-order traversal: process the tree one level at a time using a queue and count how many levels you complete. This uses O(w) space where w is the widest level, which is safer than recursion on very deep trees where the call stack would overflow.

title: Level Order Traversal — Breadth-First Over a Binary Tree
metaDescription: Watch a queue drive level order traversal of a binary tree in real C++, including how to separate levels correctly and why null children must be skipped.
intro: Depth-first traversal follows one branch to the bottom before looking at the next; level order visits everything one row at a time. That difference is entirely down to which structure holds the pending nodes, and swapping a stack for a queue is the whole implementation.
code: n->val = v; n->left = NULL; n->right = NULL;
codeNote: A fixed array with head and tail indices acts as the queue, so the whole visit order stays on screen instead of being consumed and discarded.

howItWorks.heading: The queue enforces the level ordering
howItWorks.body: A node's children are enqueued behind every node already waiting, all of which are at the same depth or shallower. FIFO therefore guarantees that depth d is fully drained before any node at depth d+1 is dequeued.

howItWorks.heading: levelSize snapshots the current row
howItWorks.body: Measuring the number of pending nodes before the inner loop captures exactly one level, because the enqueues that follow belong to the next level. Without that snapshot the loop cannot tell where one row ends.

howItWorks.heading: head advances instead of erasing
howItWorks.body: Dequeuing moves an index forward, which is O(1). Erasing from the front of a container shifts every remaining element and is O(n). Here the nodes simply stay in the array, so the finished traversal order is still there to inspect afterwards.

howItWorks.heading: Null children are filtered at enqueue time
howItWorks.body: Checking before pushing keeps the queue free of nulls so the dequeue side needs no guard. The alternative — pushing nulls and checking on dequeue — is what you want if you need to print placeholders for missing children.

howItWorks.heading: The loop ends when the queue is drained
howItWorks.body: head < tail is true exactly while unprocessed nodes remain, since tail marks where the next arrival goes and head marks the next departure. Every node is enqueued once and dequeued once, so the loop runs n times regardless of tree shape.

complexity.space: O(w) where w is the widest level
complexity.note: Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once; the memory is bounded by the widest level, which for a complete tree is about n/2 — meaning level order can use substantially more memory than a depth-first traversal on wide trees, and much less on deep ones.

gotchas.title: Measuring the level length inside the inner loop
gotchas.body: tail grows as children are enqueued, so a loop bounded by the live length tail - head never ends the level — it keeps consuming nodes from deeper rows and every level after the first is wrong. Snapshot levelSize before the inner loop starts.

gotchas.title: Dequeuing with erase(q.begin())
gotchas.body: If you back the queue with a vector and pop by erasing the front, every remaining element shifts on each removal and an O(n) traversal becomes O(n squared). On a wide tree with tens of thousands of nodes that is the difference between instant and visibly slow, for no functional gain.

gotchas.title: Enqueueing null children
gotchas.body: Pushing cur->left unconditionally puts nulls in the queue, and the next dequeue crashes on cur->val. Either filter on the way in, as here, or check for null immediately after dequeuing — but do one of them consistently, not half of each.

gotchas.title: Using a stack and expecting level order
gotchas.body: Swapping the queue for a stack silently produces a depth-first order that still visits every node, so the output looks like a valid traversal and is simply the wrong one. If your levels are interleaved, check which end of the container you are removing from.

faq.q: What is level order traversal of a binary tree?
faq.a: A breadth-first walk that visits all nodes at depth 0, then all at depth 1, and so on. It is implemented with a queue: dequeue a node, output it, and enqueue its children. This is the traversal you want for printing a tree by rows or finding the shallowest node matching a condition.

faq.q: How do you separate levels in a level order traversal?
faq.a: Record the queue's size before processing each level and dequeue exactly that many nodes. Everything enqueued during that inner loop belongs to the next level, so the count cleanly delimits the current row. Reading the size inside the loop instead of before it is the classic bug.

faq.q: Why does level order traversal use a queue instead of a stack?
faq.a: Because FIFO ordering guarantees that nodes are processed in the order they were discovered, and nodes at depth d are all discovered before any node at depth d+1. A stack reverses that, processing the most recently discovered node first, which produces a depth-first traversal instead.

faq.q: What is the space complexity of level order traversal?
faq.a: O(w), where w is the maximum number of nodes on any single level. For a complete binary tree the bottom level holds roughly half the nodes, so this is O(n) — noticeably worse than the O(h) of a recursive depth-first traversal on a balanced tree, and much better on a deep skewed one.

title: BFS Visualization — Why Breadth-First Search Finds Shortest Paths
metaDescription: Run BFS on a real graph in C++ and watch the frontier expand ring by ring. Learn why marking on enqueue matters and when BFS gives shortest paths.
intro: BFS explores a graph in rings: everything one step away, then everything two steps away, and so on. That expanding-frontier behaviour is not a side effect — it is a guarantee, and it is precisely why BFS finds shortest paths on unweighted graphs while depth-first search does not.
code: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) cout << dist[i] << ' ';
codeNote: dist doubles as the visited marker — a value of -1 means undiscovered, which removes the need for a separate boolean array.

howItWorks.heading: The queue is the frontier
howItWorks.body: At any moment the queue holds nodes at distance d and d+1 from the source, in that order. Dequeuing in FIFO order means you never process a node at distance d+1 before finishing every node at distance d.

howItWorks.heading: First discovery is shortest
howItWorks.body: Because the frontier expands outward one ring at a time, the first time you reach a node is via a shortest path. That is the entire correctness argument for BFS shortest paths, and it fails the moment edges have different weights.

howItWorks.heading: Mark on enqueue, not on dequeue
howItWorks.body: Setting dist[v] the moment v is discovered stops it being enqueued again by another node in the same ring. Marking on dequeue instead lets a node sit in the queue several times, which is still correct but can blow the queue up to O(E) entries.

howItWorks.heading: Distances come free
howItWorks.body: dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 works because u is being processed at the moment v is discovered, and u already holds its final distance. No extra pass is needed to compute the layer numbers.

howItWorks.heading: Every edge is examined once per direction
howItWorks.body: The outer loop dequeues each node once and the inner loop walks its adjacency list. Summed over all nodes, that is exactly E iterations for a directed graph, giving the O(V + E) bound.

complexity.note: Every vertex enters the queue once and every adjacency entry is scanned once, so the cost is proportional to the graph's size rather than its shape; the space is the queue plus the distance array, and the queue peaks at the size of the widest ring.

gotchas.title: Marking visited on dequeue instead of enqueue
gotchas.body: If the check happens when a node comes off the queue, a node with many in-edges gets enqueued once per neighbour before it is ever processed. The result is still correct but the queue can hold O(E) entries, and on a dense graph that is a memory blowup rather than a wrong answer — which makes it hard to spot in tests.

gotchas.title: Using BFS on a weighted graph
gotchas.body: BFS counts edges, not weights. On a graph where one edge costs 100 and a two-edge path costs 2, BFS confidently reports the wrong shortest path. If any edge weight differs from any other, you need Dijkstra — or, for 0/1 weights, a deque-based variant.

gotchas.title: Dequeuing with erase(q.begin())
gotchas.body: This shifts the whole vector on every pop, turning an O(V + E) traversal into O(V squared). It is functionally correct, which is why it survives code review, and it is the single most common reason a BFS solution times out.

gotchas.title: Forgetting to mark the source
gotchas.body: If dist[0] is left at -1, the source can be rediscovered through a cycle and re-enqueued, and on a graph with a cycle back to the start you get an infinite loop. Watching node 0 reappear in the queue is the fastest way to see it.

faq.q: Why does BFS find the shortest path?
faq.a: Because it processes nodes strictly in order of distance from the source: every node at distance d is dequeued before any node at distance d+1. The first time a node is discovered, it must therefore be via a minimum-edge-count path. This guarantee holds only for unweighted graphs, where every edge counts the same.

faq.q: What is the difference between BFS and DFS?
faq.a: BFS uses a queue and explores level by level, discovering nodes in order of increasing distance from the source. DFS uses a stack (usually the call stack) and follows one path as deep as it goes before backtracking. BFS finds shortest paths on unweighted graphs; DFS is better for cycle detection, topological sorting, and connectivity questions.

faq.q: What is the time complexity of BFS?
faq.a: O(V + E) — every vertex is enqueued and dequeued once, and every edge is examined once from its source. The V term covers the vertices themselves and the E term covers scanning the adjacency lists. Using the wrong container for the queue, such as erasing from the front of a vector, silently degrades this to O(V squared).

faq.q: Can BFS be used on a weighted graph?
faq.a: Not for shortest paths, unless every edge has the same weight. BFS minimises the number of edges, which only equals minimum total weight when all weights are equal. For general non-negative weights use Dijkstra; for graphs where all weights are 0 or 1, a double-ended queue variant of BFS works.

title: DFS Visualization — Watch the Recursion Descend and Backtrack
metaDescription: Run depth-first search on a real graph in C++ and watch the call stack grow and unwind. Covers the missing visited check that turns a cycle into a hang.
intro: Depth-first search commits: it picks a neighbour, follows it as far as it goes, and only backtracks when the path is exhausted. The recursion makes it three lines shorter than BFS and considerably harder to picture, because the interesting state lives in the call stack rather than in a container you can print.
codeNote: The graph deliberately contains a cycle (3 back to 0) so the visited check is doing real work rather than being decoration.

howItWorks.heading: The call stack is the path
howItWorks.body: At any moment, the sequence of active frames is exactly the path from the source to the node being explored. Backtracking is not a separate mechanism — it is what happens when a call returns and control resumes in the frame below.

howItWorks.heading: Mark before you recurse
howItWorks.body: visited[u] = 1 is the first statement in the function, before any neighbour is followed. If it came after the loop, a cycle would send you straight back into an unmarked node and recurse forever.

howItWorks.heading: The loop resumes where it left off
howItWorks.body: When dfs(v) returns, the for loop in u's frame continues with the next neighbour. That preserved loop index is the state that makes backtracking work, and it is stored implicitly in the stack frame rather than in any variable you wrote.

howItWorks.heading: Visited prevents revisiting, not just cycles
howItWorks.body: Even in an acyclic graph, two different paths can reach the same node. Without the check you would explore that node's entire subgraph twice, turning linear work into exponential on a graph shaped like a diamond lattice.

howItWorks.heading: One call per node, one scan per edge
howItWorks.body: Each node is entered exactly once thanks to the visited array, and each entry scans its adjacency list once. That is the O(V + E) bound, identical to BFS despite the completely different visit order.

complexity.note: Each vertex is visited once and each edge examined once, but the space is the recursion depth, which on a long path-shaped graph is V — a graph with a million nodes in a chain will overflow the call stack before it finishes.

gotchas.title: Marking visited after the recursive calls
gotchas.body: Putting visited[u] = 1 below the loop means a cycle re-enters u while it is still unmarked, and the recursion never terminates. In DryRun you see the same node id reappearing on frame after frame as the stack grows — a far faster diagnosis than reading a stack trace after the crash.

gotchas.title: Stack overflow on deep graphs
gotchas.body: Recursive DFS uses one frame per node on the current path. A graph that is essentially a long chain — common in generated test data — needs V frames, and at a few hundred thousand nodes the process dies with no useful error. Convert to an explicit stack if depth can be large.

gotchas.title: Confusing visited with on-the-current-path
gotchas.body: For cycle detection in a directed graph, a single visited flag is not enough: a node reachable by two different paths is visited but not part of a cycle. You need three states — unvisited, in progress, and done — and only an edge back to an in-progress node indicates a cycle.

gotchas.title: Forgetting disconnected components
gotchas.body: One call to dfs(0) only reaches nodes connected to 0. If the graph has several components, you must loop over all vertices and start a fresh DFS from any that are still unvisited. Silently missing half the graph is easy when your test input happens to be connected.

faq.q: How does depth-first search work?
faq.a: It starts at a source node, marks it visited, and recursively explores the first unvisited neighbour as deeply as possible before backtracking to try the next one. The recursion's call stack holds the current path, and returning from a call is exactly what backtracking means.

faq.q: Why does DFS need a visited array?
faq.a: To stop it revisiting nodes. In a cyclic graph, following edges without checking leads back to a node already on the path and the recursion never terminates. Even in an acyclic graph, the array prevents re-exploring a node reachable by multiple paths, which can otherwise turn linear work into exponential.

faq.q: Should DFS be recursive or iterative?
faq.a: Recursive is shorter and clearer, and it is fine when the graph's longest path is modest. Use an explicit stack when depth can reach into the hundreds of thousands, since each recursive call consumes a stack frame and the default stack will overflow. The two produce the same set of visited nodes but not necessarily the same visit order.

faq.q: When should I use DFS instead of BFS?
faq.a: For cycle detection, topological sorting, finding connected components, and any backtracking search over configurations. DFS also uses less memory on wide graphs, since it stores only the current path rather than an entire frontier. Use BFS instead whenever you need shortest paths in an unweighted graph.

title: Dijkstra's Algorithm — Shortest Paths, Step by Step
metaDescription: Watch Dijkstra settle nodes one at a time on a real weighted graph in C++. Learn why it needs non-negative weights and what greedy actually means here.
intro: Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly commits to the closest node it has not yet settled, then relaxes its outgoing edges. The commitment is permanent, and the fact that this is safe rests entirely on one assumption — no negative weights — which is worth understanding rather than memorising.
code: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) cout << dist[i] << ' ';
codeNote: The O(V squared) adjacency-matrix version — slower than a heap on sparse graphs, but every step is explicit and the shortest route to node 1 is via node 2, not the direct edge.

howItWorks.heading: dist holds best-known, not final
howItWorks.body: Until a node is settled, dist[v] is the shortest distance using only settled nodes as intermediates. It can improve many times. The moment a node is chosen as the minimum, that tentative value becomes final.

howItWorks.heading: Pick the closest unsettled node
howItWorks.body: The inner selection loop finds the unsettled node with the smallest tentative distance. This is the greedy choice, and the whole algorithm is that choice repeated V times.

howItWorks.heading: Why the greedy choice is safe
howItWorks.body: Any other route to u would have to leave the settled set through some unsettled node x, and dist[x] >= dist[u] by choice of u. With non-negative weights, the rest of that path can only add more, so no shorter route exists. Negative edges break this argument outright.

howItWorks.heading: Relaxation propagates improvements
howItWorks.body: For each neighbour v, if reaching v through u is cheaper than the current best, record it. This is the only place dist ever changes, and it is why a node's distance can drop several times before it settles.

howItWorks.heading: Unreachable nodes stay at INF
howItWorks.body: If the minimum unsettled distance is still INF, no remaining node is reachable and the loop can stop. Without that break, INF + weight overflows and produces nonsense distances that look like real answers.

complexity.time: O(V squared) here, O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap
complexity.note: The dominant cost is finding the minimum unsettled node V times; a priority queue replaces that linear scan with a log-time extraction, which is a large win on sparse graphs and no win at all on dense ones where E approaches V squared.

gotchas.title: Negative edge weights give wrong answers silently
gotchas.body: Dijkstra settles a node permanently, so a negative edge discovered later can offer a cheaper route that is never applied. There is no crash and no warning — just a distance that is quietly too large. Use Bellman-Ford when negative weights are possible.

gotchas.title: INF plus a weight overflowing
gotchas.body: If INF is INT_MAX and you compute dist[u] + w[u][v] for an unreachable u, the addition wraps to a large negative number that beats every real distance. Either break out when the minimum is INF, as here, or use an INF small enough that INF + maxWeight still fits.

gotchas.title: Relaxing edges out of an already-settled node
gotchas.body: With a lazy priority queue, the same node can be extracted more than once with stale distances. Without a check that skips entries where the popped distance exceeds dist[u], you redo work and, on some formulations, corrupt results. Watching a node get processed twice is the tell.

gotchas.title: Confusing not-yet-settled with unreachable
gotchas.body: A node with a finite dist that is not yet in the settled set still has a tentative value that may improve. Reading dist[v] as a final answer before the algorithm finishes gives an overestimate. Only distances of settled nodes are final at any given moment.

faq.q: Why doesn't Dijkstra's algorithm work with negative weights?
faq.a: Because it permanently settles a node the moment it becomes the closest unsettled one, assuming no later path can be shorter. That assumption relies on every additional edge making a path longer. A negative edge can make a longer route cheaper, and since the node is already settled, the improvement is never applied. Use Bellman-Ford instead.

faq.q: What is relaxation in Dijkstra's algorithm?
faq.a: Checking whether going to a neighbour v through the current node u is cheaper than v's best known distance, and updating it if so. The test is dist[u] + weight(u,v) < dist[v]. It is the only operation that ever changes a distance, and a node may be relaxed many times before it is settled.

faq.q: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm?
faq.a: O(V squared) with a simple array scan to find the minimum, or O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap. The heap version is much faster on sparse graphs where E is close to V, while the array version is competitive on dense graphs where the linear scan is no worse than maintaining the heap.

faq.q: What is the difference between Dijkstra and BFS?
faq.a: BFS minimises the number of edges and works only when every edge counts equally; Dijkstra minimises total weight and handles any non-negative weights. BFS uses a plain FIFO queue, while Dijkstra needs a priority queue to always pick the closest frontier node. On a graph where all weights are 1, Dijkstra reduces to BFS.

title: Detecting a Cycle in a Directed Graph — The Three-Colour Method
metaDescription: See why a single visited flag cannot detect cycles in a directed graph, and watch the three-state DFS get it right on real running C++.
h1: Cycle Detection in a Directed Graph
intro: The obvious approach — flag nodes as visited and cry foul when you meet one again — is wrong, and wrong in a way that passes most test cases. A node can be reachable by two separate paths without any cycle existing. The fix is to distinguish between nodes you are currently inside and nodes you have already finished.
codeNote: State 0 is unvisited, 1 is on the current DFS path, and 2 is fully explored — the diamond 0 to 1 and 2 to 3 would fool a single visited flag, while the 3 to 1 edge is the real cycle.

howItWorks.heading: Three states, not two
howItWorks.body: Unvisited means never seen. State 1 means the DFS entered this node and has not returned yet, so it is on the current path. State 2 means the node and everything below it is finished. Only state 1 indicates a cycle.

howItWorks.heading: A back edge is the definition of a cycle
howItWorks.body: Reaching a node that is still in state 1 means you have found an edge pointing back to an ancestor on the current path — which, combined with the path itself, forms a directed cycle. Nothing else in a DFS can create one.

howItWorks.heading: State 2 nodes are safe to re-encounter
howItWorks.body: Finishing a node means its entire reachable subgraph has been explored with no cycle found. Meeting it again from a different branch tells you nothing new, so the DFS skips it. This is exactly the case a single visited flag gets wrong.

howItWorks.heading: The mark flips back on exit
howItWorks.body: Setting state[u] = 2 after the loop is what removes u from the current path. Forget it and every previously explored node stays marked as on-path, so the next branch that touches it reports a phantom cycle.

howItWorks.heading: Every component needs a start
howItWorks.body: The loop in main launches a DFS from every still-unvisited node, because a cycle can live in a component unreachable from node 0. Nodes finished by an earlier DFS are skipped by the state check, so the total work is still linear.

complexity.note: One DFS over the whole graph, with each node entered once and each edge examined once; the space is the state array plus a recursion stack that can reach V frames on a long path.

gotchas.title: Using one boolean visited flag
gotchas.body: On the diamond 0 to 1, 0 to 2, 1 to 3, 2 to 3, the second path reaches an already-visited node 3 and a boolean check reports a cycle that does not exist. The graph is a perfectly valid DAG. Cross edges to finished nodes are normal; only edges to in-progress nodes matter.

gotchas.title: Forgetting to set state to 2 on the way out
gotchas.body: If the node stays at 1 after its DFS completes, it looks like it is still on the path forever. Every later branch that touches it reports a cycle, so the function returns true on almost any graph. Stepping through and watching the state array after each return exposes this immediately.

gotchas.title: Applying the directed algorithm to an undirected graph
gotchas.body: In an undirected graph, every edge is traversable both ways, so u to v and immediately v to u looks like a back edge and every single edge reports a cycle. Undirected cycle detection must skip the edge you arrived on by tracking the parent node.

gotchas.title: Starting from only one node
gotchas.body: A single call to hasCycle(0) misses cycles in components that node 0 cannot reach. The loop over all vertices is not optional, and its absence produces false negatives on exactly the graphs where a cycle matters most.

faq.q: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
faq.a: Run a depth-first search that tracks three states per node: unvisited, currently on the DFS path, and fully finished. If you ever follow an edge to a node that is currently on the path, you have found a back edge and therefore a cycle. Finishing a node moves it out of the on-path state so it stops triggering false positives.

faq.q: Why isn't a visited flag enough to detect a cycle?
faq.a: Because visited conflates two different situations: a node you are still inside, and a node you have already finished. Reaching a finished node just means it was reachable by more than one path, which is completely normal in an acyclic graph. Only reaching a node that is still on the current recursion path proves a cycle exists.

faq.q: How is cycle detection different in an undirected graph?
faq.a: In an undirected graph every edge can be walked both ways, so the edge you arrived on always leads back to a visited node. You detect a cycle by tracking the parent and reporting only when you reach a visited node that is not the parent. The three-colour method is for directed graphs specifically.

faq.q: What is a back edge?
faq.a: An edge from a node to one of its ancestors in the current depth-first search tree — that is, to a node whose DFS call has started but not yet returned. Combined with the tree path from that ancestor down to the current node, a back edge closes a directed cycle. A graph is acyclic exactly when a DFS finds no back edges.

title: Topological Sort — Kahn's Algorithm, Visualized
metaDescription: Watch in-degrees drop to zero and drive a topological sort in real C++. Learn how the same algorithm detects cycles and why the output is not unique.
intro: Given a set of tasks with dependencies, produce an order in which each task comes after everything it depends on. Kahn's algorithm does it by repeatedly taking whatever currently has no unmet dependencies — and as a free bonus, if it ever runs out of such tasks with work remaining, it has proved your dependency graph has a cycle.
code: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) order.push_back(i);
else for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) cout << order[i] << ' ';
codeNote: The order vector doubles as the queue and the result, so the finished ordering is still there to inspect rather than being consumed.

howItWorks.heading: In-degree counts unmet dependencies
howItWorks.body: indeg[v] is the number of prerequisites v still has. A node with in-degree zero has nothing blocking it and can be emitted immediately. The whole algorithm is a bookkeeping exercise on this one number.

howItWorks.heading: Emitting a node releases its dependents
howItWorks.body: When u is placed in the order, every edge u to v is satisfied, so indeg[v] drops by one. A node joins the ready set at the exact moment its last prerequisite is emitted — not before, and only once.

howItWorks.heading: Each node is enqueued exactly once
howItWorks.body: The push happens only on the transition to zero, which occurs once per node. That is why the ready set never contains duplicates and why the loop is linear.

howItWorks.heading: A short output means a cycle
howItWorks.body: If some nodes never reach in-degree zero, they are all waiting on each other. The loop stops with fewer than n emitted, which is a proof of a cycle rather than a heuristic — a DAG always admits a full ordering.

howItWorks.heading: The order is not unique
howItWorks.body: Whenever several nodes have in-degree zero simultaneously, any of them may go next. Different container choices produce different valid orderings, so tests that compare against one fixed expected sequence are testing the wrong thing.

complexity.note: Building the in-degree array scans every edge once and the main loop scans every edge once more, so the cost is linear in graph size; the space is the in-degree array plus the ready set, both bounded by V.

gotchas.title: Pushing when in-degree is merely low rather than zero
gotchas.body: Writing if (indeg[v] <= 0) or pushing before the decrement enqueues a node while it still has unmet dependencies, producing an order that violates the constraints. Worse, a node can be pushed twice and appear twice in the output. The push belongs strictly inside the transition to exactly zero.

gotchas.title: Treating a short result as success
gotchas.body: If you print the order without checking its length against n, a cyclic graph produces a partial ordering that looks entirely plausible. The size check is the cycle detector, and skipping it turns a hard error into silently wrong output.

gotchas.title: Counting out-degree instead of in-degree
gotchas.body: It is easy to increment indeg[u] instead of indeg[adj[u][i]] when building the array. The algorithm then starts from sinks rather than sources and produces a reversed or nonsensical order. On a symmetric test graph it can even look correct.

gotchas.title: Expecting one specific valid order
gotchas.body: With several ready nodes at once, any of them is a legal next choice. Swapping the ready set from a queue to a stack changes the output entirely while both remain correct. If you need determinism, use a min-heap to always take the smallest id, and say so explicitly.

faq.q: What is a topological sort?
faq.a: A linear ordering of a directed graph's vertices such that every edge points forwards — if there is an edge from u to v, then u appears before v. It models dependency resolution: build systems, course prerequisites, and task schedulers all need one. Only directed acyclic graphs have a topological order.

faq.q: How does Kahn's algorithm work?
faq.a: It counts each node's in-degree, starts with every node whose in-degree is zero, and repeatedly emits one of them. Emitting a node decrements the in-degree of each of its successors, and any successor that reaches zero joins the ready set. The process runs until the ready set empties.

faq.q: How does topological sort detect cycles?
faq.a: If the algorithm finishes with fewer than V nodes emitted, the remaining nodes form a cycle. Every node in a cycle depends on another node in that cycle, so none of their in-degrees can ever reach zero. This makes Kahn's algorithm a cycle detector at no extra cost.

faq.q: Is the topological order unique?
faq.a: Usually not. Any time two or more nodes have in-degree zero simultaneously, either can legitimately come next, so most graphs admit many valid orderings. The order is unique only when there is exactly one ready node at every step, which means the graph contains a Hamiltonian path.

title: How Recursion Actually Works — Watch the Call Stack
metaDescription: See stack frames pushed and popped in real running C++. What actually happens when a function calls itself, and why the base case is not optional.
intro: The confusing thing about recursion is not that a function calls itself — it is that several copies of the same function are alive at once, each with its own private variables, all waiting on the one above. Once you can see those frames stacked up and collapsing back down, the mystery evaporates and never returns.
codeNote: factorial stores the recursive result in a named local so the pending multiplication is visible in the frame while the deeper calls run.

howItWorks.heading: Each call gets its own frame
howItWorks.body: Calling factorial(5) creates a frame holding n = 5. The nested call creates a separate frame with n = 4. Both exist simultaneously and neither can see the other's n — that independence is what makes recursion work at all.

howItWorks.heading: The caller is suspended, not finished
howItWorks.body: When factorial(5) reaches the recursive call, it stops mid-statement. The multiplication n * sub has not happened yet and will not happen until the inner call returns a value. Five frames pile up before a single multiplication occurs.

howItWorks.heading: The base case is the only exit
howItWorks.body: if (n <= 1) return 1; is the sole path that returns without recursing. Without it, or with a condition the arguments never satisfy, frames accumulate until the stack is exhausted and the process dies.

howItWorks.heading: Results flow back down the pile
howItWorks.body: The deepest frame returns 1, which lets the frame above compute 2 * 1, which lets the next compute 3 * 2, and so on. Watching each frame wake up, receive its value, and finish is the single most useful thing you can do for your understanding of recursion.

howItWorks.heading: Every recursive call must make progress
howItWorks.body: factorial(n - 1) and sumDigits(n / 10) both move strictly towards the base case. If an argument can stay the same or move away, the recursion is unbounded regardless of how correct the base case looks.

complexity.note: One frame per pending call means recursion depth is a real memory cost, not a bookkeeping detail; a recursion that is linear in depth will overflow the default stack somewhere around a few hundred thousand frames, long before it runs out of time.

gotchas.title: A base case the arguments never hit
gotchas.body: if (n == 0) in factorial looks fine until someone calls factorial(-1), which recurses to -2, -3, and downward forever. Use n <= 1 or validate the input. Test the boundary and one step past it, not just the happy path.

gotchas.title: Recursing without changing the argument
gotchas.body: Calling helper(n) instead of helper(n - 1) inside itself produces an identical frame every time. In a step-through this is unmistakable: the same parameter value on frame after frame, growing until the crash. Reading the code for the same bug can take much longer.
