gotchas.title: Expecting a local variable to persist across calls
gotchas.body: int count = 0; inside a recursive function is reinitialised in every frame, so it never accumulates anything. If you need shared state, pass it by reference or return it up the chain — do not reach for a static, which then leaks between separate top-level calls.

gotchas.title: Treating stack overflow as a logic error
gotchas.body: A crash with no output often means the recursion simply went too deep, not that the algorithm is wrong. Recursive quicksort on sorted input, DFS on a long chain, and naive tree recursion on a degenerate tree all fail this way. The fix is an iterative version or a bound on depth, not a change to the recurrence.

faq.q: What is a base case in recursion?
faq.a: The condition under which the function returns a value directly instead of calling itself. It is what stops the recursion — every recursive call must eventually reach it. A missing or unreachable base case means frames pile up until the call stack is exhausted and the program crashes.

faq.q: Why does recursion use more memory than a loop?
faq.a: Because every pending call keeps a stack frame alive, holding its parameters, local variables, and the position to return to. A loop reuses one set of variables, while a recursion n levels deep holds n complete frames simultaneously. That is the O(n) space cost people mean when they say recursion is expensive.

faq.q: What causes a stack overflow?
faq.a: Recursion that goes deeper than the call stack can hold — either because of a missing base case, an argument that never approaches it, or a legitimately deep recursion on a large input. The default stack is typically a few megabytes, which runs out somewhere in the hundreds of thousands of frames.

faq.q: Is recursion slower than iteration?
faq.a: Usually somewhat, because each call has the overhead of setting up and tearing down a frame. The bigger cost is memory. Compilers can eliminate that overhead for tail-recursive functions by turning them into loops, but factorial as written here is not tail recursive — the multiplication happens after the call returns.

title: Fibonacci Memoization — From Exponential to Linear, Visualized
metaDescription: Watch naive Fibonacci recursion explode into thousands of calls, then see memoization collapse it to n. Real C++, real call counts, real recursion tree.
intro: Naive recursive Fibonacci is the standard demonstration of why some recursions are catastrophically slow, and it earns the reputation: fib(40) makes over 300 million calls to compute 41 distinct values. Memoization fixes it with three extra lines, and seeing the recursion tree before and after is the fastest route to understanding what dynamic programming actually buys you.
codeNote: The calls counter makes the saving concrete: memoized fib(30) reports 59 calls, while deleting the two memo lines pushes the same counter to 2,692,537.

howItWorks.heading: The naive tree is exponential
howItWorks.body: fib(n) calls fib(n-1) and fib(n-2), each of which branches again. The tree has roughly 1.6 to the power n nodes, and the same subproblems appear in it thousands of times — fib(5) alone is recomputed from scratch on nearly every branch.

howItWorks.heading: There are only n distinct subproblems
howItWorks.body: Despite the enormous tree, the function only ever has n+1 possible arguments. The explosion is entirely redundant work, which is exactly the condition under which memoization applies.

howItWorks.heading: Check the cache before recursing
howItWorks.body: The memo lookup sits above the recursive calls, so a cached value short-circuits an entire subtree. That is where the saving comes from — not from the storage itself, but from the branches that never execute.

howItWorks.heading: Store before returning
howItWorks.body: Assigning to memo[n] and then returning it guarantees the value is available to every later caller. Computing the sum and returning it without storing gives you correct answers at full exponential cost, which is a bug that produces no wrong output at all.

howItWorks.heading: The tree becomes a path
howItWorks.body: With memoization, each value is computed once on the way down and reused on the way back. The recursion tree collapses into a single spine of n calls with n cheap cache hits hanging off it — visible immediately if you compare the two call counts.

complexity.space: O(n) for the table plus O(n) stack
complexity.note: Each of the n subproblems is computed exactly once and every other call is an O(1) lookup; the naive version's cost is the size of the recursion tree, which grows by the golden ratio at each level and is why fib(50) is unreachable without a cache.

gotchas.title: Using 0 as the not-computed sentinel
gotchas.body: fib(0) is legitimately 0, so a memo initialised to 0 treats a real answer as a cache miss and recomputes it forever. Worse, in problems where 0 is a common valid result, the cache silently stops working and you get exponential behaviour with correct output. Use -1, or a parallel boolean array.

gotchas.title: Sizing the memo to n instead of n + 1
gotchas.body: The table must be indexable at n itself. Off by one and the top-level call writes past the end of the vector — undefined behaviour that frequently appears to work because the vector has spare capacity.

gotchas.title: Computing but not storing
gotchas.body: return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); with the lookup still present looks memoized and is not. The cache is read but never written, so every lookup misses. The output is still right, so nothing looks wrong until you compare step counts — running both versions in DryRun and seeing one finish in 59 calls and the other not finish at all settles it immediately.

gotchas.title: Overflowing int at around fib(47)
gotchas.body: Fibonacci numbers grow exponentially and pass 2 billion at index 47. With int return values you get silent wraparound to negative numbers. Use long long, and be aware that even that runs out around index 92.

faq.q: What is memoization?
faq.a: Caching the result of a function call so that repeating the same call returns the stored value instead of recomputing it. It applies when a function is pure — the same arguments always produce the same result — and when the same arguments recur. It turns a recursion's cost from the size of its call tree into the number of distinct subproblems.

faq.q: Why is naive recursive Fibonacci so slow?
faq.a: Because it recomputes the same values an exponential number of times. fib(n) branches into two calls that overlap almost entirely, producing a tree with about 1.6 to the power n nodes to compute only n distinct values. fib(40) makes over 300 million calls; memoized, it makes 79.

faq.q: What is the difference between memoization and tabulation?
faq.a: Memoization is top-down — you write the natural recursion and add a cache, so only the subproblems actually needed get computed. Tabulation is bottom-up — you fill a table in dependency order with loops, no recursion and no stack depth. They have the same asymptotic cost; tabulation avoids stack overflow, memoization avoids computing unreachable states.

faq.q: Why initialise the memo array to -1 instead of 0?
faq.a: Because 0 is a valid Fibonacci value, so it cannot double as a marker for not-yet-computed. Using it as a sentinel means fib(0) is never cached and the cache check misfires. Choose a sentinel outside the function's possible range, or keep a separate array of booleans.

title: Climbing Stairs — Bottom-Up DP in Two Variables
metaDescription: Solve climbing stairs with bottom-up dynamic programming in real C++, see why the answer is Fibonacci, and how to cut the DP table down to two integers.
intro: You can climb one or two steps at a time — how many distinct ways are there to reach step n? The recurrence falls out of a single observation about the last move you made, and the resulting solution needs no array at all once you notice that each answer depends on only the two before it.
codeNote: Rolling two variables instead of an n-element table; the printed sequence 1 2 3 5 8 13 21 34 is Fibonacci shifted by one.

howItWorks.heading: Reason about the last step, not the first
howItWorks.body: Any route to step n ends with either a 1-step or a 2-step move. Those two cases are disjoint and cover everything, so ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). Framing the recurrence by the final decision is a habit that generalises to most counting DP problems.

howItWorks.heading: The base cases are counts, not indices
howItWorks.body: There is exactly 1 way to reach step 1 and 2 ways to reach step 2 (1+1 or 2). Getting these wrong shifts the entire sequence, and since the shifted sequence is still Fibonacci it still looks plausible.

howItWorks.heading: Bottom-up means no recursion at all
howItWorks.body: Because state i depends only on smaller states, a simple ascending loop fills them in dependency order. There is no call stack, so this version cannot overflow no matter how large n gets.

howItWorks.heading: Two variables replace the table
howItWorks.body: The recurrence reaches back exactly two positions, so nothing older than that is ever needed again. prev1 and prev2 slide forward each iteration, cutting memory from O(n) to O(1) without changing a single result.

howItWorks.heading: The assignment order matters
howItWorks.body: cur must be computed before prev2 is overwritten, and prev2 must take the old prev1 before prev1 is updated. Reorder those three lines and the sequence silently becomes powers of two.

complexity.note: One addition per step with no table at all; the naive recursive formulation of the same recurrence is exponential for exactly the reason naive Fibonacci is, since it recomputes overlapping subproblems instead of reusing them.

gotchas.title: Off-by-one base cases
gotchas.body: Returning 1 for n = 2 instead of 2 shifts the whole sequence down by one, and because the result is still a Fibonacci number the output looks reasonable. Verify by hand: two steps can be climbed as 1+1 or as 2, so the answer is 2.

gotchas.title: Updating prev1 before prev2
gotchas.body: Writing prev1 = cur; prev2 = prev1; makes prev2 take the new value rather than the old one, so both variables end up equal and the sequence becomes 1, 2, 4, 8. Watching the two variables after each iteration makes the doubling obvious within two steps.

gotchas.title: Solving it recursively without memoization
gotchas.body: The naive recursion is a one-liner and takes exponential time, so n = 45 hangs. If your solution is correct on small inputs and times out on large ones, this is almost always why. Either memoize or use the loop.

gotchas.title: Integer overflow past n = 46
gotchas.body: The count grows like Fibonacci, exceeding the range of a 32-bit int at around n = 46 and wrapping to a negative number. Use long long if n can be large, and note that no amount of DP correctness saves you from an overflowing accumulator.

faq.q: Why is climbing stairs the same as Fibonacci?
faq.a: Because both satisfy the recurrence f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2). Every route to step n ends with a move of either 1 or 2 steps, so the total splits into routes to step n-1 and routes to step n-2. The only difference from standard Fibonacci is the starting values, which shift the sequence by one position.

faq.q: How do you solve climbing stairs in O(1) space?
faq.a: Keep only the last two counts in two integer variables and slide them forward on each iteration. The recurrence never looks back further than two positions, so the rest of the DP table is dead weight. Update the older variable from the newer one before overwriting the newer one.

faq.q: What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up here?
faq.a: Top-down writes the recursion with a memo table and computes states on demand, using O(n) stack depth. Bottom-up starts at the base cases and loops upward, using no stack at all. For this problem bottom-up is strictly better — the dependency order is trivially known, so there is nothing to gain from recursion.

faq.q: What if you can climb 1, 2 or 3 steps at a time?
faq.a: The recurrence becomes f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) + f(n-3), producing the tribonacci sequence, and you carry three rolling variables instead of two. The same reasoning extends to any fixed set of allowed step sizes: sum the counts for each possible last move.

title: 0/1 Knapsack — Reading the DP Table Cell by Cell
metaDescription: Fill a 0/1 knapsack DP table in real C++ and see what each cell means. Covers the take-or-skip recurrence and why the 1D version must loop backwards.
intro: Given items with weights and values and a bag that can hold a limited weight, maximise what you carry. The greedy instinct — take the best value-per-kilo first — is provably wrong here, and the reason it fails is exactly what makes the DP table necessary.
codeNote: Rows are items and columns are capacities; the answer 9 comes from taking the weight-3 and weight-4 items, not the highest-value one.

howItWorks.heading: Every cell is a complete subproblem
howItWorks.body: dp[i][c] is the best value achievable using only the first i items with capacity exactly c available. Being able to state that sentence precisely is the difference between writing DP and copying it.

howItWorks.heading: The decision is take or skip
howItWorks.body: For item i you either leave it, inheriting dp[i-1][c], or take it, gaining its value plus the best solution for the remaining capacity using only earlier items. The maximum of those two is the answer for that cell.

howItWorks.heading: Why the recurrence looks back a row
howItWorks.body: Both branches read from row i-1 because each item may be used at most once. Reading from row i instead would allow the same item to be taken repeatedly, which is the unbounded knapsack — a different problem with a one-character difference in code.

howItWorks.heading: Row 0 and column 0 are the base cases
howItWorks.body: With no items, or no capacity, the best value is 0. Initialising the vector to zero handles both, which is why the loops can start at 1 with no special cases inside.

howItWorks.heading: Greedy fails because capacity is lumpy
howItWorks.body: The highest value-per-weight item can leave an awkward remainder that nothing fits into. In this instance the greedy pick blocks a better combination. DP works because it evaluates every capacity split rather than committing to one.

complexity.note: One constant-time decision per table cell, which is pseudo-polynomial rather than polynomial — the cost scales with the numeric value of W, so a capacity of one billion is intractable even with only ten items.

gotchas.title: Mixing up the item index offset
gotchas.body: Row i corresponds to item i-1 in the zero-indexed arrays. Writing wt[i] instead of wt[i-1] reads past the end on the last row and silently shifts every item by one. If your answer is close but consistently wrong, check this first.

gotchas.title: Looping capacity forwards in the 1D version
gotchas.body: The space-optimised version overwrites a single row in place. Iterating capacity upwards means dp[c - wt] has already been updated for the current item, so the item gets taken more than once and you have accidentally solved unbounded knapsack. The loop must run from W down to wt[i].

gotchas.title: Reading dp[i][c - wt] instead of dp[i - 1][c - wt]
gotchas.body: This is the same bug in the 2D table: it permits reusing the current item. The result is always at least as large as the correct answer, so it looks like an improvement rather than an error. Stepping through the table and checking which row a cell was read from settles it.

gotchas.title: Assuming greedy by value density works
gotchas.body: Sorting by value per unit weight and taking greedily is correct for fractional knapsack, where items can be split, and wrong for 0/1. The failure is not an edge case — it happens on small ordinary inputs like this one — and no tie-breaking rule fixes it.

faq.q: What does dp[i][c] mean in the knapsack problem?
faq.a: The maximum total value obtainable using only the first i items with a capacity of c. Each cell is a self-contained answer to a smaller version of the same question, which is why the table can be filled row by row using only previously computed cells.

faq.q: Why can't you solve 0/1 knapsack greedily?
faq.a: Because taking the item with the best value-to-weight ratio can leave a capacity remainder that nothing fits into, blocking a better combination. Greedy is correct only for fractional knapsack, where you can take part of an item and any leftover capacity is always usable.

faq.q: Why does the 1D knapsack loop go backwards?
faq.a: Because the space-optimised version reuses one array for both the previous and current item rows. Iterating capacity downwards guarantees that dp[c - weight] still holds the previous item's value when you read it. Going forwards reads an already-updated cell, which lets the same item be taken repeatedly.

faq.q: Is knapsack really polynomial time?
faq.a: It is pseudo-polynomial. The O(n * W) cost is linear in the numeric value of the capacity, not in the number of bits used to write it down, so doubling the bit-length of W squares the runtime. That is why 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard despite having a table-filling algorithm that looks efficient.
